fix(gateway): background idle compaction review fixes

- Buffered text batches are matched by the event's session, not by the batch key: adapters
  key them their own way (a sender or topic suffix, a bare chat id), so the session-key
  lookup missed a waiting message.
- The job re-checks buffered input right before summarising: it may have waited for a slot
  behind other summaries after the claim checked.
- A Codex app-server thread in `native`/`off` mode is left to compact itself: the gateway
  pipeline would force it as `/compress` does.
- Docs: a channel's `idle_compact_after_seconds` edit takes effect after a gateway restart,
  like the other `channel_overrides` fields (the primary profile reads the boot config).

fix(gateway): a due idle policy is not pre-empted by the cache edge's offload claim

Live probe: on a route that arms a prompt-cache warmer (a Claude model on a custom URL),
the first housekeeping tick past the cache window claims `offload`. The offload found
nothing to prune, and the idle check only ran when the edge claimed nothing, so the
background idle compaction landed one interval (~5 min) late, and a user back in that
window got the turn-start compaction in front of their message. The idle policy is now
checked first (scan and release); a refused compaction leaves the edge to claim on the
next tick.

feat(gateway): idle chats compact in the background on every route, per channel `compression.idle_compact_after_seconds` only ran at the start of the next turn, so the user's first message after a long idle waited for the summary, and the gateway's background compaction ran only at the prompt-cache edge, i.e. only on routes with cache keep-alives. Local models, custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints and unpriced routes never compacted in the background. - The housekeeping tick's cache-edge scan now also claims a cached chat whose idle policy has passed (`idle` action, `gateway/run_watchers_idle.py`) when its cache edge claimed nothing. It runs the same job: one per session key, the shared semaphore, the chat's profile scope and claim gate, the manual-compression pipeline (lease, fence, automatic gates, durable cooldown) with the `idle` trigger. No new worker, table or scheduler. - Before summarising, the turn-start idle gates run on the stored transcript (`idle_compaction_admission`, extracted from `_idle_compaction` so both paths share them): above the post-compaction floor, grown since the last compaction, no cooldown. - Once per idle stretch: the claim latches on the agent's last activity, so a refused or failed chat is not retried until it has new activity; a success evicts the agent. - Skips a chat with a turn running or with input an adapter has not dispatched yet (pending message, text batch, in-flight guard) or the runner queued. - A chat whose agent the idle-TTL sweep evicts first is compacted at release when due (`_compact_then_release` no longer requires a prompt-cache warmer). - Silent on the chat; the outcome goes to the gateway log. - `platforms.

.channel_overrides..idle_compact_after_seconds` overrides the global value for one channel (0 turns it off there), resolved through `_channel_override` like model/system_prompt/allow_silence and stamped on the agent every turn, so a cached agent follows config edits and the background run reads the chat's own policy. The buffered-input check follows kylebach's #128358 (`_post_reply_idle_has_pending_input`). Co-authored-by: kylebach <97074323+kylebach@users.noreply.github.com>

test(compression): run #135759's idle-reference tests on the storage-interface fixtures

The contributor's tests built their store with the deprecated SessionDB, which no longer
exposes `.sessions` on current main, so the agent's compression-recovery read raised. Use
the same `storage_handle` + `seed_session` helpers as the idle-compaction guard tests.

Co-authored-by: N0tS0Lucky <65911386+N0tS0Lucky@users.noreply.github.com>

fix(compression): measure the idle-compaction gap from the transcript, not _last_activity_ts (#79357)

Every turn entry re-stamps agent._last_activity_ts before the idle check reads
it: DurableTurnLease.start() touches activity right before run_conversation,
the gateway resets it for cached agents, and a rebuilt agent (cache eviction,
restart) starts with it at construction time. The measured gap was therefore
always ~0 and idle_compact_after_seconds never fired, on Desktop/TUI/CLI as
well as gateway.

Use the newest timestamp among the transcript rows preceding this turn's user
message as the idle reference. Transcript rows are timestamped in memory and in
state.db, so this survives all three resets uniformly. _last_activity_ts is kept
only as the fallback for untimestamped transcripts.

fix(prompt-cache): a late keep-alive reply never rewinds a newer fold

Review finding: a settled run (its request's reply already folded) checked only
the context witness, which ordinary appended turns do not change, so a keep-alive
reply landing after the NEXT request had folded was folded with its older send
time and moved the guarantee backward. It now folds only while it is the latest
send on the clock.

Part of #160322.

fix(prompt-cache): price the unmarked tail of a request in flight as input

Review finding: the request in flight was counted as fully cached, so a small
marked prefix followed by a large unmarked tool result (routes that leave tool
results unmarked) could be kept warm by replays that re-bill the tail at the full
input rate. request_split counts what follows the last cache marker as uncached.

Part of #160322.

fix(prompt-cache): order a keep-alive's renewal against its request's own reply

Review finding: the renewal of the request's attempt ran after the keep-alive's
clock fold, usage booking and log line, so the request's reply could fold in
between from the old send time; and a keep-alive whose reply landed after the
request's own reply was dropped (its run had been replaced), leaving the clock
counting from the request's send.

The loop's reply is now folded under the warmer lock (fold_reply), the same lock a
keep-alive's fold takes, and the renewal happens inside that locked fold: either
the keep-alive renews the attempt first and the reply counts from it, or the reply
folds first, marks the run settled, and the keep-alive folds after it as a later
read of the same prompt (unless a rewrite intervened). The tier the request in
flight keeps warm comes from the clock's own rule (requested_cache_tier, shared
with request_write_tier) instead of a second copy of it, and the in-flight helpers
live in agent/prompt_cache_lifecycle/in_flight.py.

Part of #160322.

fix(prompt-cache): a marked request is kept warm from its first send

A request carrying cache_control markers declares its tier (the clock's
Anthropic-spec rule), so the first long reply of a session is covered too; an
automatic cache still has to prove itself on the clock first. The prompt size
is estimated from the payload instead of the previous reply.

Part of #160322.

docs(prompt-cache): keep-alives while a reply generates

Part of #160322.

fix(prompt-cache): keep a request's prompt warm while its reply generates

A reply that takes longer than the cache entry lives (a subagent's single long
generation, a slow upstream) found its own prefix gone, and the next request
re-wrote all of it: no keep-alive could go out, because the warmer was cancelled
when the request was built and armed again only after the reply landed.

The request going out now arms a run that replays that same request before the
entry expires (start_in_flight). It needs a route an earlier reply proved caches,
counts the entry from this send for the tier the request asks, and is booked like
a tool wait (its keep-alives together cost no more than the one rewrite they
prevent; the user turn's idle budget is untouched). Each keep-alive moves the
request's attempt send time on, so the reply folds from the latest renewal instead
of moving the window back to its own send. The reply replaces the run as before;
a retry or fallback rebuilds it, the turn's end cancels it.

Fixes #160322

fix(http): keep every pinned URL when downloads finish together on Windows (#16144)

When several downloads of the same pinned file finished at once on
Windows, the download cache could forget some of the URLs it had seen
that file at. A later install from a forgotten URL then downloaded the
file again instead of reusing the cached copy. Nothing failed, but cache
reuse was lost without any message.

The cache's pin index maps a checksum pin to every URL the file was
downloaded from, so a pin is only reused for a URL it was actually
served from. Recording a URL reads the entry, adds the URL, and writes
it back under a lock. Two steps could drop URLs:

- **Reading the entry.** Any read error was treated as "no entry yet",
so the entry was rewritten with only the current URL and every earlier
URL was lost. On Windows, opening a file can briefly fail with an
access-denied or sharing error while antivirus scans it or another
process is replacing it.
- **Writing the entry.** The cache's own atomic write didn't retry the
Windows rename when it was refused for the same reason. The error was
then swallowed at debug level, so that URL was lost.

Now:

- Only a missing entry counts as empty. Other read errors are retried
for about a second on Windows lock errors (new
`file::retry_transient_lock`). If the read still fails, the entry is
left untouched rather than overwritten.

fix(npm): don't save version lists built from an old cached packument (#16148)

Commands that prefer to stay offline (`mise ls`, `hook-env`, `exec`,
`x`, `env`, …) answer `npm:` tools from the cached npm packument,
however old it is. That is fine for those commands, but mise then saved
the version list and `latest` it built from that packument to its
version caches, dated *now*. For the next `fetch_remote_versions_cache`
(1 hour by default), `mise install`, `mise latest`, `mise outdated` and
`mise upgrade` reused those days-old answers: they installed an old
`latest` and said everything was up to date.

For example, with a packument cached 8 days earlier, when `vercel` was
at 65.17.0:

```
$ mise ls npm:vercel
npm:vercel  65.17.0 (missing)  ~/proj/mise.toml  latest
$ mise install --dry-run
# before: mise npm:vercel@65.17.0 ⇢ would install
# after:  mise npm:vercel@67.0.0 ⇢ would install
$ mise latest npm:vercel
# before: 65.17.0
# after:  67.0.0
```

Now, when the npm registry client runs offline or prefer-offline, the
version list and `latest` it builds from a cached packument are used for
that command but not saved. A list or `latest` already in mise's cache
and still fresh is used as before. `npm.shell_out`, git sources and
tarball sources ask their source directly and are unchanged.

Fixes #16105

## Validation

- New e2e test `backend/test_npm_prefer_offline_stale_packument` ages a
cached packument, runs `mise ls`, and checks that no version cache is
written and that `latest`, `ls-remote` and `install --dry-run` pick the
current release.
- The reproduction script from the issue gives 65.17.0 with 2026.11.14
and the current release with this branch.
- `cargo test --lib backend::npm` and `mise run lint` (including Clippy)
pass. `backend/test_npm_aube` fails locally with exit 127 both here and
on `origin/main`.

security(backend): tighten archive extraction and stop ubi sending tokens to other hosts (#16075)

Installing a tool from a release archive could go wrong in a few ways:

- an archive's symlink could end up pointing outside the install
directory after `bin` or `rename_exe` moved it, or through a chain of
more than 40 links, and later install steps wrote through it;
- a small 7z archive could make mise hold gigabytes in memory before
extraction limits applied, and an archive full of links could keep the
link check busy for a very long time;
- the `ubi:` backend sent a GitHub or GitLab token to whatever host a
`ubi:` URL or a GitLab release link named, and treated any `api_url`
containing `github.com` as the public GitHub API;
- with `extract_all`, `mise.lock` checked one file of a `ubi:` install
and nothing else;
- a `ubi:` `exe` or `rename_exe` with `..` wrote outside the install
directory, and an archive with no visible file made mise panic.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

**Archives mise unpacks**

- **Moving symlinks for `bin` and `rename_exe`**: an archive's links are
checked where the archive puts them. Moving an executable that is a
symlink out of a macOS `.app` bundle or into a nested `bin` directory
changed what its relative target named, which could be outside the
install. mise now refuses to move a symlink to another directory:

  ```
cannot move the symlink <path> to <target>: from there its target would
name a different path. Point `bin` or `rename_exe` at the file the link
names instead.
  ```

Renames within one directory, and executables shipped as regular files,
work as before.

- **Long link chains**: the symlink check followed at most 40 links and
then accepted the link. A link that needs more than 40 links to resolve,
counting the link itself, is now refused, as the operating system
refuses to open it:

  ```
  symlink <path> in <dir> resolves through more than 40 links: <target>
  ```

A loop of links is taken as written, and the rest of the path after it
is still checked. The same applies to vfox plugin installs.

- **Time spent checking links**: the work for one install is now
bounded, so an archive whose links make every check walk thousands of
path components is refused with `the symlinks in <dir> take too long to
check (more than 20000000 steps), so the archive is refused`. Archives
with ordinary links, including absolute links into the archive's own
tree, install as before.

- **Packed 7z headers**: a 7z archive can store its header packed, and
the 7z reader unpacked it into memory before mise saw the first entry.
mise now reads the size the archive declares for a packed header and
refuses the archive before unpacking it when that is over what
`extract_max_ratio` allows:

  ```
7z header unpacks to <n> bytes, over the <max> that the
extract_max_ratio setting allows
  ```

A 7z archive with no start header is refused as well, because the reader
would search the file for a header to unpack. Setting
`extract_max_ratio` to 0 turns the check off.

**`ubi:` backend**

- **Where tokens go**: the ubi library sends its token with every
request, the download included, and reads `GITHUB_TOKEN`,
`GITLAB_TOKEN`, `CI_JOB_TOKEN`, `CODEBERG_TOKEN` or `FORGEJO_TOKEN` from
the environment when mise gives it none. mise now hands it a token only
when every request goes to the forge API, or to `github.com` for the
public GitHub API. For a `ubi:` URL on another host, or a GitLab release
whose asset links point at another host, mise gives ubi no token, and
refuses the install when one of those variables is set, because ubi
would read it:

  ```
ubi would send the GITHUB_TOKEN token to example.com, which is not the
GitHub API
hint: unset GITHUB_TOKEN, or install the tool with the github, gitlab or
http backend
  ```

For a GitLab project, mise reads the release just before the install,
with the same token ubi will send (including `CI_JOB_TOKEN`), and checks
where its asset links point.

The same refusal applies when safe mode denies a token to a project's
`api_url` and one of those variables is set.

- **Self-hosted `api_url`**: an `api_url` was taken for the public
GitHub or GitLab API when it contained `github.com` or `gitlab.com`, so
`https://github.company.example/api/v3` was dropped and the tool came
from public GitHub. The host is now matched exactly, so a self-hosted
`api_url` is used as configured. An `api_url` that is not a URL is now
an error.

- **`extract_all` checksums**: with `extract_all`, `mise.lock` held the
checksum of one file, picked by name from what the release contained.
mise now records a blake3 checksum of the whole install (every path,
file content, executable bit and symlink target) under a key ending in
`-extract_all`, and checks it on later installs.

- **`exe` and `rename_exe` paths**: a value with `..` or an absolute
path, such as `rename_exe = "../../../.bashrc"`, is now refused, as
`bin_path` already was. `bin/tool` still works.

- **Empty installs**: when ubi installed no file with the expected name
and no file whose name does not start with a dot, mise panicked. It now
fails with `ubi installed no file into <dir> whose name does not start
with a dot`.

**Docs**

- The ubi backend page says where ubi sends tokens and when mise refuses
an install, and its comparison table says that `extract_all` installs
record a checksum of the whole install.

## Compatibility

- A `ubi:` tool given as a URL on a host other than the forge API fails
while `GITHUB_TOKEN` or one of the other variables is set, which is the
usual case in CI. Unset the variable for that install, or move the tool
to the `github`, `gitlab` or `http` backend. This PR refuses because the
ubi library cannot be told to send no token; the alternatives are for
mise to download URL installs itself, or to add a "no token" option to
ubi upstream.
- An `extract_all` tool whose `mise.lock` holds a single-file checksum
fails with `mise install --locked`, and fails without `--locked` when
that entry names a file other than the one mise picks. Remove the entry
from `mise.lock` so mise records the whole-install checksum. This PR
fails closed; the alternative is to replace the old entry silently.
- `bin` or `rename_exe` that would move a symlink to another directory
now fails. Point the option at the file the link names.
- An archive with a link chain longer than 40 links, a 7z archive with a
zeroed start header, or a 7z archive whose packed header is over the
limit is refused. The link-check budget (20,000,000 steps) and the 7z
header limit (the `extract_max_ratio` limit divided by 100) are fixed,
not settings.
- A `ubi:` `exe` or `rename_exe` with `..` or an absolute path is
refused, and an `api_url` that does not parse as a URL is an error.

## Validation

Each fix has unit tests, and most were seen to fail without their fix;
the archive symlink e2e test gained cases for `rename_exe` and a nested
`bin` with the `http` and `github` backends. Seven real `.7z` release
assets, including 7-Zip, Notepad++ and Node.js archives, passed the
packed-header check and extracted. A tampered `extract_all` release and
the token refusal against a real foreign host were not tested end to
end.

security(config): limit what a project .miserc.toml can select and stop rendering untrusted settings (#16083)

A `.miserc.toml` found from the current directory loads before config
and trust, so a cloned repository's copy takes effect as soon as you
`cd` into it. Several of its keys reached further than a project file
should:

- its `ignored_config_paths` replaced the list from your global
`miserc.toml`, so a checkout under an ignored directory could un-ignore
itself;
- the environments it selected also loaded
`~/.config/mise/config.<env>.toml` and `/etc/mise` files, and their
names reached `{{ mise_env }}` in trusted config unchecked;
- its override filenames could name files such as `.netrc` in any
directory mise searches, home included;
- its globs, lists and malformed values could crash every command in the
project or stall each prompt.

Separately, `netrc_file = "~/..."` was read relative to the current
directory, and the prompt hook rendered the templates in an untrusted
project's `[settings]`.

This PR fixes each of those. Your global and system `miserc.toml`, `-E`
and `MISE_ENV` keep working as before.

## What changes

**Project `.miserc.toml`**

In this section, a project file is a `.miserc.toml`,
`.miserc.local.toml` or `.config/miserc.toml` found from the current
directory, or `~/.miserc.toml`.

- **`ignored_config_paths`**: a project file adds its entries to the
list it inherits from the global and system files and from parent
directories, and cannot remove one, so `ignored_config_paths = []` no
longer un-ignores a checkout. The global and system files still replace
each other's list, and `MISE_IGNORED_CONFIG_PATHS` still replaces them
all.
- **Environment names**: names in a project file's `env` and `env_sets`
may use only letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`, starting with a letter
or digit, since they reach every config's templates as `mise_env`. Any
other name is ignored with a warning:

  ```
ignoring environment "<name>": a name in a project .miserc.toml may use
only letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`, starting with a letter or digit;
select it with -E or MISE_ENV instead
  ```

- **Global per-environment config**: an environment a project file
selects, through `env`, `env_sets` or `auto_env`, loads the project's
own `config.<env>.toml` files only. `~/.config/mise/config.<env>.toml`
and the matching `/etc/mise` files load only when the global or system
`miserc.toml`, `-E`, `MISE_ENV` or `MISE_AUTO_ENV` selects that
environment. Before, a project could load one of those files, which need
no trust and can set `yes` or `paranoid`, or skip one by turning
`auto_env` off. The same holds in mise commands that mise starts, such
as through `mise x` or a task, also in another directory: they use every
active environment in `MISE_ENV` for that directory's config files, and
your own selection for the global ones. A config filename with a
directory that your global `miserc.toml` lists, such as
`.config/mise/custom.toml`, still loads.
- **Override filenames**: a name in a project file's
`override_config_filenames` must be a file name without a directory that
ends in `.toml`, and one in `override_tool_versions_filenames` must end
in `tool-versions`. Other names are ignored with a warning such as:

  ```
ignoring override filename ".config/mise.toml": a name in a project
.miserc.toml must be a file name, without a directory; set it in
~/.config/mise/miserc.toml instead
  ```

In the global `miserc.toml`, any name that stays in its directory still
works.
- **Long lists**: mise uses only the first 64 entries of a project
file's `env` and of each override filename list, and the `env_sets` of
all project files may name 64 environments between them; a set that
would go past that is ignored. mise warns about what it leaves out, for
example `using only the first 64 of the 2000 entries in env`. The
filename lookup also uses a set instead of comparing lists entry by
entry. mise caps the lists before it checks the names, and gives one
warning per list and reason that names every entry it drops.

**Everywhere**

- **`netrc_file`**: a path that starts with `~/` now names a file in
your home directory. A relative path is ignored with a warning, and no
netrc file is used:

  ```
ignoring netrc_file x/netrc: it is not an absolute path, so mise is not
using a netrc file. Set netrc_file to an absolute path or one that
starts with ~/
  ```

Before, `~/.netrc` was looked up as a directory named `~` under the
current directory.
- **Config globs**: an `ignored_config_paths` or override filename
pattern longer than 4096 bytes or with more than 64 `{`, or one the glob
library cannot compile, no longer crashes mise with `regex compilation
shouldn't fail`. An `ignored_config_paths` entry that cannot be compiled
is treated as a literal path, as an invalid glob already was; a filename
pattern is skipped with `failed to compile config glob pattern …`.
- **TOML parse errors**: a value that spans more than 20 lines is marked
on its first line only, an excerpt over 4 KiB falls back to the one-line
`<file>:<line>:<column>: <message>` form, and the parser's message is
cut at 4096 characters and 20 lines. Before, a long multi-line value of
the wrong type printed every line and took time that grew with the
square of the file's size. Shorter errors print as before.
- **`[settings]` templates in the prompt hook**: to find out whether
`unix_default_inline_shell_args` is set, which mise does before an
`exec()` template or an enter hook from the global config, mise now
reads only the global and system config. That setting can only be set
there, so the answer is the same. Before, the check parsed every
discovered config, and parsing rendered the templates in a project's
`age.key_file`, `age.identity_files`, `age.ssh_identity_files` and
`dotfiles.root`. Under `MISE_SAFE=1`, `mise settings` also no longer
renders those templates from a project file:

  ```
not rendering <label> in <file>: safe mode does not render templates
from project config; run without MISE_SAFE to show it
  ```

The docs for `.miserc.toml`, environments, error excerpts, security and
`netrc_file` describe the new rules.

## Compatibility

- A project `.miserc.toml` can no longer select an environment name with
other characters, such as `foo+bar` or `.hidden`. Select it with `-E`,
`MISE_ENV` or the global `miserc.toml`.
- An environment a project selects no longer loads
`~/.config/mise/config.<env>.toml` or `/etc/mise` files. Select it with
`-E`, `MISE_ENV` or the global `miserc.toml` to load those too.
- An override filename with a directory, such as `.config/mise.toml`, or
one with another ending, now has to be set in
`~/.config/mise/miserc.toml`.
- A project file with more than 64 environments or override filenames
uses the first 64, with a warning. This PR uses a fixed limit of 64; the
alternative is a higher number or a setting.
- A relative `netrc_file` is ignored with a warning instead of being
read from the current directory.
- Long TOML parse errors print shorter.
- Under `MISE_SAFE=1`, `mise settings` warns and shows a project file's
templated age, dotfiles and write_targets path settings as written,
unrendered; the file's other settings still show.

## Validation

Each change has a new e2e test that failed without it, plus unit tests
for the environment name and override filename rules, the list limit,
`netrc_file`, the glob limits and the error excerpts; the existing
`miserc`, `netrc`, safe mode and TOML error e2e tests pass. The full
unit and e2e suites were not run, and nothing was tested on Windows.

security: keep dotfiles, bootstrap and daemon imports from acting on files other users control (#16089)

`[dotfiles]`, `[bootstrap.repos]`, `mise bootstrap remote` and daemon
imports could act on files that another user controls:

- git ran with its ownership check turned off, so a checkout another
user owned could run commands from its `.git/config` as the user running
mise, often root;
- as root, a symlinked parent directory owned by another user could send
a dotfile write, edit, removal or clone anywhere, including root-only
directories;
- a remote bootstrap loaded a `mise.toml` that any user of the target
had left in `/tmp`;
- a wildcard dotfile entry turned a backslash in a unix file name into a
separator, so a file could be deployed outside the directory the entry
names;
- a daemon imported with `project =` loaded an untrusted
`.tool-versions` or `.node-version` above that project;
- a dotfile meant to be `0600` was briefly readable by other users while
it was written;
- a remote host could make `mise bootstrap remote` or `mise ssh` buffer
output until it ran out of memory.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

- **Git ownership check**: `[bootstrap.repos]` and dotfile entries with
`manifest = "git"` passed `-c safe.directory=<path>` (or
`safe.directory=*`) to every git command, which turned off git's check
for repositories owned by another user. The check now stays on. `mise
bootstrap repos status` reports such a checkout as a conflict naming
`safe.directory`, with `git refuses a repository that another user owns;
see git's safe.directory setting`, and apply stops before changing
anything. A git manifest whose source another user owns fails with git's
dubious ownership error.
- **Symlinked parents as root**: when mise runs as root, `[dotfiles]`
entries, dotfile groups and `[bootstrap.repos]` now follow the rule
`[bootstrap.files]` already had: a symlinked parent is followed only
inside a root-owned directory no other user can write. Any other one is
refused in status, dry run, apply, unapply and group prune, and again
right before each change:

  ```
its path crosses symlink <path>, which root does not follow outside a
root-owned directory no other user can write; declare the resolved path
instead
  ```

A repository whose checkout path crosses such a link is a conflict.
Nothing changes for mise run as any other user.
- **Remote bootstrap config search**: `mise bootstrap remote` unpacks
the project under `/tmp/mise-bootstrap.*/project` on the target, and
config search there walked up through `/tmp`. The remote command now
sets `MISE_CEILING_PATHS` to the staging directory whenever the
bootstrap runs from it (a staged source or the `--adopt` preview), so
nothing above the staged project is loaded. A real `--adopt` bootstrap
still runs in the target's global config directory with its own
settings.
- **Backslashes in wildcard dotfile entries**: an entry with `**` in its
source and target turned every backslash in a matched name into a slash
on every platform, so a source file named `..\mise\conf.d\zz.toml`
expanded to `~/.config/app/../mise/conf.d/zz.toml`. Backslashes are now
separators only on Windows; on unix such a file is deployed as one file
with that name inside the target directory, as directory-walking entries
already did.
- **Daemon imports from another project**: a daemon imported with
`project =` loads the whole config hierarchy of the project it names,
but only that hierarchy's `mise.toml` files had to be trusted. Every
file of the hierarchy, including a `.tool-versions` or an idiomatic
version file such as `.node-version` in a parent directory, must now be
trusted unless the current project already loaded it; a project nested
inside the current one is checked the same way:

  ```
daemons in <project> need <file>, which is not trusted; run `mise trust
<file>` after reviewing it
  ```

- **Dotfile file modes**: copy, template and `content` targets were
written with the umask's mode (usually `0644`) and got their declared
`permissions` afterwards, so a file meant to be `0600` was briefly
readable by others, who could keep reading it after the chmod.
Templates, `content`, and copies that set `permissions` are now created
readable only by their owner and get their final mode once their content
is written, and a copy written over an existing file whose new mode
shuts out a current reader is replaced by a new file, so a handle opened
on the old one never sees the new content. The new file keeps the old
file's owner and group, and is written beside the target and renamed
into place, so a copy that fails leaves the old file; mise refuses a
target it cannot write, or whose owner it cannot keep. A copy without
`permissions` still uses a plain file copy, which already has its final
mode and keeps metadata such as macOS extended attributes.
- **Remote output**: `mise bootstrap remote` and `mise ssh` read each
short answer from the host (home directory, platform, mise path and
version) in full. Each answer's stdout and stderr are now read up to 1
MiB; a host that writes more on either stream fails the command at once
with `remote command on '<host>' wrote more than 1048576 bytes of
output`, and the ssh process is stopped, even if the other stream stays
open.

## Compatibility

- A checkout or git manifest source owned by another user, such as in a
container, CI job or on a drive without ownership, is now a conflict or
an error. If you trust it, add it once with `git config --global --add
safe.directory <path>`. `sudo mise` on the invoking user's own checkouts
keeps working, because git honours `SUDO_UID`.
- As root, a target or checkout path that crosses a symlink in a
directory another user can write is refused for that entry, and `mise
dotfiles apply` fails the plan. Declare the resolved path instead.
- A remote bootstrap from a staged project sets `MISE_CEILING_PATHS` for
the remote mise, replacing one you set for that run. This PR replaces
it; the alternative is to append the staging directory to yours, which
keeps your ceilings.
- An untrusted `.tool-versions` or idiomatic version file above a
project you import daemons from now blocks the import or start until you
run `mise trust` on it, even when it holds no templates. This PR
requires trust for every file; the alternative is to require it only for
files with templates or env directives, which is a content-based
exception to trust. A project nested inside the current one gets the
same check for the files the current project did not load.
- On unix, a backslash in a wildcard target pattern is a literal
character, as it already was in a non-wildcard target.
- Final file modes are unchanged.

## Validation

Unit tests cover the root symlink rule, backslash expansion, owner-only
creation of copies, templates, `content` and fnox targets, daemon import
trust and the remote output limit, and the repos, dotfiles, remote
bootstrap and daemon import e2e tests gain cases for each change.
Fifteen e2e tests were run and pass. Comparing old and new builds as a
normal user: backslash names stay inside the entry's directory, final
modes match, a checkout's `core.fsmonitor` no longer runs, the daemon
import is refused until `mise trust`, and a planted parent config is not
loaded. In a throwaway container as root, writes, edits, removals and
clones through another user's symlinked parent are now refused. Not
verified: a remote target running an older mise on macOS.

security(github): run credential commands from your home directory and bound OAuth and relay traffic (#16080)

The commands and connections mise uses to get and lend GitHub tokens
trusted their surroundings more than they should have:

- `credential_command`, `oauth_cache_get` and `oauth_cache_set` ran in
the directory mise was called in, so inside an untrusted clone the
programs they started (git, `python3 -m`, `gh` on Windows) could load
that project's config or code;
- the host passed to `credential_command` could hold characters that
`cmd` or another shell would act on;
- a slow or oversized reply from the GitHub OAuth server could hang
`mise hook-env`, and its verification URL went to the system opener
unchecked;
- the token relay that `mise bootstrap` lends over ssh could be filled
with connections that never sent anything, and the staging path a remote
host returned went into the forwarded socket path unchecked;
- a checkout pinned to a commit SHA could write another commit's files
through a replace ref brought along by the clone.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

- **Credential commands**: a github, gitlab or forgejo
`credential_command`, and `oauth_cache_get` and `oauth_cache_set`, now
run in your home directory, without `GIT_DIR` and the other git
variables, as mise already does for `git credential fill`. Before, they
ran in the current directory.
- **Credential command hosts**: mise runs `credential_command` only for
a host spelled like a DNS name or an IP address, optionally with a port
(letters, digits, `.`, `-`, `_`, and `[`, `:`, `]` for IPv6). For any
other host it moves on to the next token source. Before, a host taken
from a project's URL could add to a command line that expands
`%MISE_CREDENTIAL_HOST%`.
- **GitHub OAuth replies**: the device-code, polling and refresh
requests are limited to `http_timeout` for the whole exchange, and their
replies to 64 KiB. Before, the client's read timeout restarted with
every byte, so a server that trickled out a reply could hold the prompt
indefinitely, since a refresh runs from `mise hook-env`. A refresh that
hits either limit fails like any other failed refresh and leaves the
cached token as it was.
- **OAuth verification page**: with `github.oauth_open_browser`, mise
opens the device flow's verification URI only when it parses as an https
URL, and passes it in normalized form. On Windows it uses `rundll32
url.dll,FileProtocolHandler` instead of `cmd /C start`. Otherwise mise
still prints the URL and code for you to open by hand.
- **Bootstrap token relay**: when the relay is full and a new client
connects, it closes the oldest connection that has not yet presented the
relay's capability. Connections that did present it are never closed to
make room. Before, connections that sent nothing could block every later
request from the bootstrap.
- **Bootstrap staging path**: after `/tmp/mise-bootstrap.`, mise accepts
only letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, which is everything `mktemp`
writes. Any other path stops the bootstrap with:

  ```
  remote mktemp returned an unsafe staging path: "<path>"
  ```

Before, a path containing `${VAR}` or `%` tokens reached the socket path
given to `ssh -R`, which OpenSSH expands from mise's own environment.
- **Pinned git checkouts**: a git source pinned to a commit SHA (a
plugin, a tool built from git, a bootstrap repo) is checked out with
`--no-replace-objects`, so the files on disk are the pinned commit's.
Git commands mise runs in your own repositories are unchanged.

## Compatibility

- A `credential_command`, `oauth_cache_get` or `oauth_cache_set` that
reads a relative path now reads it from your home directory. Use an
absolute path if it relied on the project directory.
- A host that isn't a plain host name skips `credential_command` and
falls through to the next token source with only a debug log line. The
alternative is a warning, which this PR does not add.
- OAuth requests now fail once `http_timeout` has passed in total, not
per read. This PR reuses `http_timeout`; the alternative is a separate,
longer limit for OAuth.
- A GitHub Enterprise server whose verification URI is plain `http://`
no longer opens a browser automatically; the URL is still printed. This
PR accepts https only; the alternative is to also open http URLs.
- A pinned checkout no longer applies replace refs.

## Validation

Each fix has a unit test that failed without it: the replace-ref
checkout with both git and gix, the credential command's directory and
host check, the OAuth reply size and deadline, the https-only
verification URL, the relay at its connection limit and the staging
path. No e2e tests were added. The Windows and macOS browser-opening
code was not compiled or run, the Windows `cmd` path was not exercised,
and the relay was tested at the listener level, not through a full
bootstrap.

fix(shim): keep shims of installed tools that enable_tools or disable_tools exclude (#16139)

A `mise install` or `mise reshim` run with `MISE_ENABLE_TOOLS` or
`MISE_DISABLE_TOOLS` no longer deletes the shims of other installed
tools.

Before, a deploy script that ran `MISE_ENABLE_TOOLS=node,bun mise
install` on a shared machine left only the node and bun shims in
`~/.local/share/mise/shims`. Every other installed tool's shim (`gh`,
`jq`, …) was deleted, and anything that called them failed with exit 127
until someone ran a plain `mise reshim`:

```
$ mise ls --installed
jq     1.8.1
shfmt  3.12.0
$ MISE_ENABLE_TOOLS=jq mise install
$ ls ~/.local/share/mise/shims
jq                # before: shfmt deleted
jq  shfmt         # after
```

`enable_tools` and `disable_tools` narrow what one command uses, often
only through an environment variable. The shims directory serves every
process, so a tool these settings exclude now keeps its shims for as
long as it is installed. Uninstalling it still removes them. This
follows the earlier fixes that stopped reshim from deleting the shims of
another project's tools (#14277) and of `path:` tools.

This also applies to a `path:` tool that another project configures.
Previously a reshim under `MISE_DISABLE_TOOLS` removed its shims; now it
keeps them. `disable_backends` is unchanged: tools of a disabled backend
type still get no shims.

Fixes #16069

## Notes

- Reshim now lists the bins of installed tools that the filters exclude.
For an asdf plugin, that runs the plugin's `list-bin-paths`, as an
unfiltered reshim already does.
- A shim kept for an excluded tool behaves like any shim with no active
version: in a process where the tool is filtered out, it falls back to
PATH or reports that no version is set.

## Test plan

- New e2e `e2e/cli/test_reshim_tool_filters`: with two installed tools,
filtered `install`, `reshim` and `reshim --force` keep both shims. After
an uninstall, the shim is removed.
- `e2e/cli/test_reshim_path_version`: a `path:` tool that
`MISE_DISABLE_TOOLS` excludes now keeps its shim after `reshim --force`.
- Ran the issue's reproduction script against the debug build: it prints
`jq shfmt` on every line.
- `mise run lint` and `cargo test -p mise --lib shims` pass.

fix(lock): lock per-tool python in locked mode and keep it on mise lock <tool> (#16138)

Fixes #16067.

A pypi/pipx tool can pick its own Python (`"pypi:black" = { version =
"25.9.0", python = "3.12" }`), and that Python is locked as an ordinary
`python` entry. `mise lock` handled those entries differently from every
other entry, so it broke in two ways.

**Locked mode couldn't add them.** With `tool_config.locked = true` (or
`MISE_LOCKED=1`), `mise lock` is the way to add entries, but it failed
as soon as a tool selected a Python the lockfile didn't have yet. It
also wrote no lockfile, and its hint said to run `mise lock`:

```
mise ERROR failed to resolve selected Python dependency python@3.12 for lockfile mise.lock
mise ERROR python@3.12 is not in the lockfile
```

Now it adds the per-tool Python just as it adds tools and a global
`python`. This covers the first lock, adding a tool, changing a tool's
`python`, `mise lock <tool>`, and task tools.

**`mise lock <tool>` dropped other tools' Pythons.** With black on
`python = "3.12"` and ruff on `python = "3.13"`, `mise lock pypi:ruff`
left only the 3.13 entry, so `mise lock --check` then failed with
`python@3.12 is not in the lockfile`. This happened without locked mode
too. Now the Pythons that other tools select keep their existing
entries. They aren't re-resolved, so `mise lock --bump pypi:ruff`
doesn't move black's Python, and a tool that isn't locked yet doesn't
get an entry. This covers config tools, tool stubs and task tools. `mise
lock python` still re-locks all of them.

In locked mode, `mise lock` also no longer prints `Failed to resolve
tool version list for <tool>: ... is not in the lockfile` for entries it
is about to add. `mise install` and `mise lock --check` still reject a
missing entry.

- New cases in `e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_pipx_selected_python`: `mise
lock <tool>` keeps another tool's Python, and locked mode adds a
per-tool Python without the warning and locks a changed one. The `mise
lock <tool>` case fails without the fix.
- `test_lockfile_tool_config_locked`, `test_lockfile_locked_mode`,
`test_lockfile_generate_tool_config_locked`,
`test_lockfile_generate_tool_config_locked_install` and
`test_lockfile_check` pass.

run the full e2e suite.

fix(npm): stop npm.shell_out version lookups re-entering mise through a foreign node shim (#16136)

With `npm.shell_out = true`, looking up an `npm:` tool's versions could
start a runaway loop of `node` and `npm view` processes. This happened
when another mise's shims directory was first on `PATH`, for example a
test runner that points `HOME` at a temp dir while
`~/.local/share/mise/shims` stays on `PATH`. On a Debian machine it grew
to thousands of processes and hit the process limit.

#14084 already stopped mise from running that foreign `npm` shim and
picked the system npm instead. But mise still gave that npm a `PATH`
with the foreign shims directory first. Debian's `/usr/bin/npm` starts
with `#!/usr/bin/env node`, so it found the shims directory's `node`,
which ran mise again. That run did another `npm view` for every `latest`
npm tool, and so on.

mise now removes from the child `PATH` every directory whose `node` is
the running mise binary, so the npm script finds the real `node`. A
directory where only `npm` is a mise shim stays on `PATH`, so a real
`node` beside it (as in a shared `/usr/local/bin`) is still found. The
same applies to the `npm --version` check mise runs to detect npm
features.

**Before** (the reporter's repro: a foreign shims dir, then a system npm
that uses `#!/usr/bin/env node`):

```text
$ mise ls-remote npm:semver
mise ERROR …/sys-bin/npm exited with non-zero status: exit code 42
```

The fake `node` shim, which exits 42 instead of re-entering mise, was
the `node` that ran.

**After:** with the foreign `node` a symlink to mise, as in a real shims
directory, the same setup lists the versions and the system `node` runs.

### Not covered

The shell-out `npm install` builds its `PATH` from the toolset and still
runs `npm` by bare name. Its `PATH` puts the toolset's own `node` first,
so in practice this loop starts at version lookup, which happens before
install. Removing foreign shims from the install `PATH` is not part of
this PR.

### Testing

- New unit tests: an npm that starts with `#!/usr/bin/env node` next to
a foreign `node` shim; a directory with only a `node` shim; a directory
with a mise `npm` shim beside a real `node`, which stays; and a `PATH`
with no shims, which stays unchanged.
- Ran the issue's repro against a debug build: before the fix the
foreign `node` shim runs; after it the system `node` runs and
`ls-remote` succeeds.
- `e2e/backend/test_npm_shell_out_foreign_shim` and `mise run lint`
pass.

Fixes #16066

docs(security): say which resource exhaustion is in the threat model (#16133)

The [threat model](https://mise.jdx.dev/security.html#threat-model)
covered project-config trust, tools and plugins, and running commands.
It never said whether making mise hang or run out of memory counts as a
security bug. Reporters and reviewers had no line to point to when a
report or PR adds a bound on some input.

This adds a **Resource exhaustion** item to the threat model and a
matching paragraph to `SECURITY.md` under *Reporting a vulnerability*.

**In scope:** input that mise reads before you trust it, or that comes
from the network, must not make mise hang, crash, or use unbounded
memory, disk or CPU. That covers:

- project config, `.tool-versions` and `mise.lock` you have not trusted,
and any `.miserc.toml`, including what `mise activate` reads when you
`cd` into a repository you just cloned
- anything mise reads in safe mode (`MISE_SAFE=1`)
- remote metadata: version lists, release APIs, checksum lists, registry
templates and OAuth responses
- downloaded archives: decompression bombs and archives with too many
entries, even when download verification passes

**Out of scope:** trusted config and the tools and tasks it runs.
Trusted config can already run commands as you, so a trusted config that
loops or allocates a lot is an ordinary bug, not a vulnerability. The
same goes for a large tool you chose to install.

Docs only; no behavior changes.

## Validation

- `hk run check` on both files (oxfmt, markdownlint) and `git diff
--check` pass
- `mise run docs:build` passes, and the new item's anchors
(`#configuration-trust`, `#safe-mode`, `#download-verification`) and the
`/cli/activate.html` link resolve in the built site
- `cargo test -p mise --bin mise docs_commands` passes
- No TOML blocks changed, so `schema_matches_parser` was not run

fix(lock): stop remote task files from failing install and lock on Windows (#16132)

On Windows, `mise install` and `mise lock` failed in any project with a
task whose `file` is remote (`git::...` or `https://...`):

```toml
[tasks.hello]
file = "git::https://github.com/jdx/mise.git//xtasks/show-output-on-failure?ref=v2026.11.12"
```

```
Error:
   0: The filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect. (os error 123)
Location:
   src\cli\lock.rs:568
```

`mise install` hit this when it updated the lockfile after installing
tools, so setting `lockfile = false` fixed `install`, but `mise lock`
still failed. Linux and macOS were not affected.

**Cause:** before writing the lockfile, mise reads each config file and
task file so it can tell if one changes during the run. Install and lock
don't download remote tasks; that only happens when a task runs. So a
remote task's `file` was still its URL, and mise tried to read the URL
as a local path. On Linux and macOS that read reports "not found" and is
skipped. On Windows the `:` and `?` make the name invalid, and the error
stopped the command.

**Fix:** remote task files that haven't been downloaded are left out of
that check. They aren't local files, so nothing is lost by skipping
them. `install` and `lock` now ignore remote tasks on Windows, as they
already did on Linux and macOS.

Fixes #16053

### Testing
- New unit test: remote (`git::`, `https://`) task files are left out of
the files mise reads before writing the lockfile; local task files are
still included.
- `mise run lint:clippy` passes.
- Not tested on Windows itself.

fix(install): hold install output while a confirmation prompt is open (#16134)

Fixes #16064.

When `mise install` runs a source build (e.g. a `cargo:` tool) in
parallel with an npm package that triggers a supply-chain confirmation
(`… looks suspicious`, `… is newly registered`), the build's output used
to print straight through the open prompt:

```text
cargo:https://github.com/russellbanks/komac@branch:main    Compiling zlib-rs v0.6.8
@actions/languageserver looks suspicious: 935 downloads last week (threshold: 1000). Continue adding @actions/languageserver?


   Yes     No

←/→ toggle • y/n/enter submit
cargo:https://github.com/russellbanks/komac@branch:main    Compiling anstream v1.0.0
```

Worse, a build line could erase the prompt's Yes/No menu and let the
progress display redraw over the prompt until it was answered.

Now, output that other installs print while a prompt is open is held
back and printed, in order, as soon as the prompt is answered. The same
applies while mise hands the terminal to an elevated (`sudo`) child.

### Cause

The prompt paused mise's progress renderer, but build lines (child
stderr → `SingleReport::println`) went to clx's `ProgressJob::println`,
which ignores the pause: it clears what it thinks is the progress frame
(at that moment, the prompt), writes the line, un-pauses the renderer,
and redraws the frame.

### Change

`MultiProgressReport` now queues output from `println` (TTY and text
install reporters, `ProgressReport`, `VerboseReport`) while any pause
guard is held, and flushes it when the last guard drops. The check and
the write happen under the same lock as the pause, so a prompt can't
start between them.

### Validation

- New unit test `output_is_held_until_every_pause_is_released` covers
nested pauses and ordering.
- `cargo test -p mise-ui --lib` and `mise run lint` (including Clippy)
pass.
- Not reproduced end-to-end with a real npm prompt during a cargo build.

Not addressed here: aube can ask twice about the same package (new name,
then low downloads); and clx's `println` should itself respect an
existing pause.

security(config): narrow what an untrusted project's tool versions and lockfile can make mise do (#16092)

A project's tool list and `mise.lock` load without trust, so mise has to
treat what they say as data. In several places it let them do more:

- a `ref:` or `rev:` version, which can name any commit the forge
serves, loaded without trust, and an untrusted lockfile could pin one;
- an untrusted lockfile could move a tool onto a fallback backend from
the registry, such as an asdf plugin, and its checksums alone made aqua,
github and node skip the provenance check;
- a `pypi:` version such as `1.0.0/x` reached pip or uv as a path,
resolved from the project directory;
- a native shim installed every missing tool of the project, not only
the one you ran;
- in safe mode, `mise lock` passed a `pypi:` tool's `install_env` to uv;
- a few inputs crashed or corrupted things: a tool key such as `"cargo:"
= "1"` made every prompt panic, a very long version panicked java and
ubi, `mise x` mangled arguments that are not UTF-8, the cleanup of
install directories named after a URL login matched by name alone, and
`mise use` on a templated `.tool-versions` wrote the rendered values,
secrets included, back into the file.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

**Trust**

- **`ref:` and `rev:` versions**: a `ref:` or `rev:` version (and the
`ref-` / `rev-` forms) in `mise.toml`, `.tool-versions` or an idiomatic
version file now needs trust, like a `path:` version. An untrusted
`mise.lock` entry that locks one is ignored with:
  ```
<file> locks <tool> to <version>, which needs its config to be trusted;
ignoring the entry. Run `mise trust` to use it
  ```
`tag:` and `branch:` versions load without trust as before. In safe mode
the version is kept, since safe mode loads the config untrusted anyway.
- **Lockfile backend**: until the project is trusted, mise takes a lock
entry's backend only when it is the one the registry selects for that
version. An entry for a backend the registry lists only as a fallback is
ignored with a warning that the entry needs trust, as entries for other
backends already were.
- **Lockfile provenance**: a checksum lets aqua, github and node skip
the provenance check only when it comes from a trusted lockfile and has
the URL it was recorded with. The checksums of an untrusted lockfile,
and a checksum recorded without its URL, are still compared with every
download, but provenance is checked as it would be without a lockfile.
For node, locked or not, a checksum without its URL is compared first
and then `SHASUMS256.txt` and its signature are checked.

**pipx and uv**

- **Versions that are paths**: a `pypi:` version may hold only the
characters a PEP 440 version or a `1.*` match uses, and must not end in
an archive extension. Anything else fails before pip or uv runs:
  ```
pypi:ruff: "2.6.0/x" is not a PyPI version; set a release version such
as 1.2.3 in the config
  ```
pipx and uv now also run in the tool's install directory instead of the
current directory.
- **`install_env` while locking in safe mode**: `MISE_SAFE=1 mise lock`
no longer passes a `pypi:` tool's `install_env` to uv. It warns `using
tool-level install_env for pypi:<tool> is disabled in safe mode
(MISE_SAFE=1)` and locks that tool's version without a dependency graph.
Installing already refused the option in safe mode; that check now runs
before any package manager starts, for direct callers such as
`install-into` too.

**Shims and exec**

- **Native shims**: a shim that is not mise itself (the Windows exe and
file modes, and the scripts reshim writes for an asdf plugin's shims)
now installs only the configured tool that provides the command, as a
symlink shim does. Before, with auto-install on, running one installed
every missing tool in the project's config. `mise exec` typed by you
still installs them all.
- **Arguments that are not UTF-8**: `mise x -- cmd <arg>` passes
trailing arguments on unchanged. Before, invalid bytes were replaced
with U+FFFD.

**Robustness**

- **A key with no tool name**: a key such as `"cargo:" = "1"` is
reported as naming no tool instead of making `mise hook-env` panic on
every prompt. This covers every backend prefix.
- **Very long versions**: a java or ubi version too long for the
matching regex matches nothing instead of panicking.
- **Install directories named after a URL login**: the cleanup of
install directories whose names carry URL credentials removes a
directory only when the install state records it as that tool. Before, a
crafted tool key could remove another tool's installs.

**`.tool-versions` with templates**

- **Templates kept on edit**: when `mise use`, `mise unuse` or `mise
upgrade --bump` edits a `.tool-versions` that has templates, the lines
it does not change are written back with their templates, including a
template line that renders to a comment or to nothing, which stays when
the tool above it is removed; on the line it changes, a version it keeps
stays as written and a new version replaces the templated ones. Before,
every line was written back rendered, so `{{ env.TOKEN }}` became the
token. Where mise cannot do that, it refuses to write:
  ```
not writing <file>: the name of <tool> is written with a template, which
mise would replace with the value it renders to. Edit the file by hand
not writing <file>: a version of <tool> is written with a template,
which mise would replace with the value it renders to. Edit the file by
hand
not writing <file>: it has a template tag, a template or a value that
spans lines, or a template that removes a line break, so mise cannot
tell which line a template renders to and would replace every template
with its value. Edit the file by hand
  ```

## Compatibility

- An untrusted project that pins a `ref:` or `rev:` version now needs
`mise trust` before that version is used.
- An untrusted `mise.lock` entry for a registry fallback backend is
ignored until the project is trusted. This PR accepts only the
registry's selected backend; the alternative is to also accept fallbacks
that run no plugin code, such as `aqua:` or `github:`.
- A checksum recorded without its URL, even in a trusted lockfile, no
longer skips provenance, so such an install verifies again. This PR
re-verifies those entries; the alternative is to keep accepting a
trusted checksum without its URL. A node mirror that does not sign
`SHASUMS256.txt` then needs `node.gpg_verify = false`.
- A `pypi:` version that is a path, URL or archive name now fails; use a
release version. pipx and uv no longer run in the project directory, so
a project `uv.toml` or a relative path in `uvx_args` or `pipx_args` no
longer applies to installs.
- In safe mode, `mise lock` records a `pypi:` tool with `install_env` by
version only, without its dependency graph.
- A native shim no longer installs the project's other missing tools as
a side effect; run `mise install` for those. This PR limits the install
and adds no trust prompt to native shims.
- An install directory named after a URL login that the install state
does not record is no longer removed automatically.
- `mise use`, `mise unuse` and `mise upgrade --bump` refuse to edit a
`.tool-versions` whose edited line names its tool with a template, where
a version it keeps may come from a template (one that renders to several
versions or joins a version written next to it, or a line with more than
one template), or that has a template tag, a template or a value
spanning lines, or a `{{- ... }}` that starts a line or a `{{ ... -}}`
that ends one; edit the file by hand.

## Validation

Each fix has a regression test, mostly new e2e tests (native shim
installs, pypi path versions, safe-mode `install_env` while locking, a
key with no tool name, non-UTF-8 arguments, templated `.tool-versions`,
untrusted lockfile provenance) plus new cases in the lockfile backend,
node GPG and cargo URL credentials tests, and unit tests for the version
check, trust rules, lockfile vouching, long versions and line-preserving
`.tool-versions` writes. The full unit and e2e suites were not run, and
the Windows path of the non-UTF-8 fix was not compiled.

security(core): require trust for project virtualenvs and install the builds mise.lock pins (#16072)

Several core tools did more with a cloned repository, a lockfile or the
system temporary directory than they should have:

- the python `virtualenv` tool option and `python.uv_venv_auto` put a
repository's own `.venv/bin` first on PATH before the project was
trusted, and also in safe mode;
- ruby, erlang and java could install something other than the archive
`mise.lock` pins, or skip its checksum;
- a line in the precompiled python index could point the download at
another GitHub repository;
- ruby-build and node source builds were staged under fixed names in the
system temporary directory, where another user on the machine could
create them first;
- a Gemfile's `ruby file:` option followed a symlink out of the project.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

- **Python virtualenvs**: a relative `virtualenv` path, and the
virtualenv of a uv project (the nearest directory with `uv.lock`), are
activated only when that exact project directory is trusted: a trusted
mise config file in it, or `mise trust <dir>`. In paranoid mode only a
trusted config file in it counts. A parent directory's `mise trust`
record no longer covers a project below it (a `trusted_config_paths`
entry or a trusted monorepo root still does), and with no project root a
relative path is not activated at all. Otherwise mise warns:

  ```
mise WARN virtualenv .venv not activated: ~/src/app is not trusted, run
`mise trust ~/src/app` to activate it
  ```

For a uv project the warning starts `uv project ~/src/app is not
trusted`. A `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT` outside the project that already
exists is still used.
- **Python virtualenvs in safe mode**: a project's virtualenv is never
activated. An absolute `virtualenv` path applies only when global or
system config, or a CLI argument, sets the option itself.
- **Python precompiled index**: a line from the list of precompiled
builds must be a whole archive name, with no `/`, `\`, `%`, `?` or `#`.
Before, a line that only started like an archive name became part of the
download URL and could reach another repository on github.com. Other
lines are now skipped.
- **Ruby and `mise.lock`**: on Linux and macOS, `mise install` downloads
the URL `mise.lock` pins when it is the precompiled archive for that
version and platform, and checks it against the locked checksum. Before,
mise asked the release API which archive to install, so a newer build
revision such as `3.4.1-1`, a moved asset or a missing release led to
another archive or a ruby-build compile without checking the lock. An
entry that keeps a checksum without its URL is still compared with the
download. Under `--locked`, an entry that pins the source tarball no
longer installs a precompiled build published later.
- **Erlang and `mise.lock`**: when `mise.lock` pins the checksum of a
precompiled build and builds.hex.pm (or the GitHub release on macOS and
Windows) no longer lists it, the install fails instead of compiling OTP
from source with kerl and rewriting the lock entry:

  ```
  precompiled erlang is not available: <reason>
mise.lock pins its checksum (<url>); refusing to compile from source
instead
  set erlang.compile = true to build from source
  ```

Without a pin, and on hosts no precompiled build is published for, the
source fallback is unchanged.
- **Java kept downloads**: with `always_keep_download`, an archive that
failed the `mise.lock` checksum stayed in the downloads directory and
the next install used it without checking. A kept archive is now checked
like a fresh one, and one that fails is deleted.
- **Source build staging**: ruby-build is fetched and its `install.sh`
run from the ruby cache directory instead of a fixed directory in the
system temporary directory. Node source builds put their patches and
build tree in a `source-build` directory under the version's cache
directory, instead of `MISE_TMP_DIR`, and remove it after a successful
build.
- **Gemfile `ruby file:`**: the named file is read only when it resolves
inside the Gemfile's directory. A symlink out of it, in the file or in a
directory of the name, is not followed, and mise warns:

  ```
mise WARN not reading ~/src/app/version named by `ruby file:` in
~/src/app/Gemfile: a symlink leads it out of the Gemfile's directory;
copy the file into the project or set the version in the Gemfile
  ```

## Compatibility

- A freshly cloned uv project, or a project picked up by a relative
`virtualenv` in global config, no longer activates its `.venv` until you
run `mise trust <dir>` on that project (in paranoid mode, trust a mise
config file in it). A subproject of a trusted project needs its own
trust.
- In safe mode, a project's virtualenv is not activated. Set an absolute
`virtualenv` in global config, or an existing `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT`
outside the project, if you need one there.
- A ruby install whose locked release was deleted now fails on the
download. Run `mise lock ruby` to move to the current build.
- An erlang install whose pinned precompiled build can no longer be
found now fails. Set `erlang.compile = true` to build from source, or
update the lock entry.
- A `.ruby-version` linked from above the project is still read by mise
under its own name, but no longer through the Gemfile, so engine options
on that Gemfile's `ruby` line don't apply to it.
- Node source builds use a `source-build` directory under the version's
cache directory for their build tree instead of `MISE_TMP_DIR`, and
remove it after a successful build.
- With a GitHub repository as the ruby precompiled source, a locked URL
is recognised by its file name, as ruby on Windows and precompiled
python already do, and its locked checksum must match. The alternative
is to also require the configured repository's host, which would reject
a lock entry pointing at a mirror.
## Validation

New e2e tests cover project virtualenv trust (including safe and
paranoid mode), the java kept download, ruby-build staging, the ruby
locked URL with a changed or missing release, and the erlang pinned
build that is no longer listed; unit tests cover the python index line,
the ruby archive URL check, the erlang lock pin and the Gemfile symlink.
Each new test failed without its fix, and the related core plugin unit
tests and e2e tests pass. Windows and the slow e2e tests were not run.

`1.4.4` and `v1.4.4`. The existing path-segment test still passes.

security(vfox): confine plugin code and downloads, and stop hook-env from installing plugins (#16093)

mise runs vfox plugins on every prompt to work out versions and
environments, before a project's config is trusted, so the code that
hosts them has to keep them to their own files and to what was locked.
In a few places it did not:

- a plugin's `require` searched the current directory first, so it could
load a Lua file or native library from the project;
- `hook-env` cloned and ran a project's backend plugin on `cd`, and ran
plugin hooks for a `system` version and for a tool plugin used as a
backend;
- a vfox tool's lockfile checksum was only checked with `--locked`, and
paranoid mode and `locked_verify_provenance` still let a lockfile entry
skip attestation checks;
- the plugins' `archiver` module wrote zip entries named `../x` outside
the destination, the vfox HTTP client had no timeout, and a PATH entry
holding `:` crashed `hook-env`.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

**Plugin code**

- **`require` search path**: a filesystem plugin's `require` now
searches only its own directory (`?.lua`, `hooks/?.lua` and `lib/?.lua`
there), an embedded plugin searches no directory, and `package.cpath` is
empty, so no native module is loaded. Before, Lua's defaults put
`./?.lua` and `./?.so` first, so a `require` of a module the plugin did
not ship loaded it from the current directory.
- **`system` versions**: `vfox:<plugin>@system` and
`<plugin>:<tool>@system` run no plugin hook for bin paths or the
environment, and count as installed whether or not the plugin is
present, since mise installed nothing for them.
- **Tool plugins used as a backend**: the backend hooks refuse a plugin
that does not ship them, before any of the plugin's Lua (`metadata.lua`
or another hook) runs:
  ```
vfox plugin <name> has no hooks/<hook>.lua, so it is not a backend
plugin and cannot be used as <name>:<tool>
  ```
Before, mise still ran the plugin's code for a hook it does not define.

**Plugin installs**

- **No install from `hook-env`**: resolving a version alias and
computing a tool's environment no longer install the backend plugin. An
alias for a plugin that is not installed resolves to nothing, and the
environment of a tool whose plugin is missing fails with:
  ```
[<plugin>] plugin not installed, so <tool>@<version> has no environment;
run `mise install` to install it
  ```
  `mise install` installs the plugin and resolves the alias again.

**Lockfile**

- **Checksums on every install**: the checksum a `mise.lock` entry
records for a vfox tool is checked on every install, not only with
`--locked`. A download that no longer matches fails with `Checksum
mismatch`. If the entry records a checksum but the plugin's PreInstall
returns no URL, the install fails, since there is nothing to check it
against.
- **Provenance under paranoid mode**: with paranoid mode's `provenance`
category or `locked_verify_provenance` on, a vfox tool's attestation is
verified on every install, even when the lockfile already records its
provenance. The recorded provenance is only restored when verification
was skipped.

**Downloads and environment**

- **Zip extraction**: the `archiver` module extracts zip files with
checks on entry names, so an entry such as `../../x` is refused and an
absolute name is never written outside the destination. The error names
the archive and the destination.
- **HTTP timeout**: the vfox HTTP clients use `http_timeout` (30 seconds
by default) to connect and between reads, so a server that stops
answering no longer hangs `hook-env`. `http_download_timeout` still
bounds the whole download.
- **PATH entries with a separator**: when a plugin's env hook returns a
key more than once, a second or later value that holds the path
separator, such as a directory named `web:app`, is skipped with a
warning instead of panicking. The first value of a key is used as
written, as before:

security(github): check release assets against every checksum list and refuse mismatched releases (#16078)

For `github:`, `gitlab:` and `forgejo:` tools, mise checks a release
asset against the checksum files the release publishes. Several cases
let an asset install without that check, or from the wrong release:

- only the first checksum file was read, even when it was a signature or
did not name the asset;
- a checksum file that failed to download, or named the asset in a form
mise could not parse, was skipped;
- a release answered for another tag was installed under the requested
version;
- `minimum_release_age` could install a newer release published under a
twin tag (`v2.0.0` for `2.0.0`);
- `mise.lock` recorded an md5 or sha1 when a sha256 list was also
available;
- a registry tool's `attestations_since` exempted numeric tags that were
not three-part semver, such as `v0.72`.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

**Locating the asset's checksum**

- **Every checksum list**: mise used the first checksum-looking file of
a release, which could be `SHA256SUMS.sig` or a list that does not name
the asset, and then installed unchecked. mise now skips signature files
and searches every checksum list the release offers.
- **Lists mise could not download**: a checksum file that failed to
download was logged and skipped. When no other list names the asset, the
install now fails:

  ```
cannot verify <asset>: the release publishes checksum files mise could
not download or read, and no other checksum file lists it:
    <file>: <error>
For a download error, check the network and the forge token, then retry.
To install anyway, pin the asset with the tool's `checksum` option.
  ```

- **Entries mise could not parse**: an entry that named the asset as
`SHA256 (file) = …`, with a `./`, `*` or directory prefix (including a
directory with spaces, but not one whose name starts with `:`), or with
a hash of the wrong length was taken as "not listed". mise now reads
coreutils and BSD-style lines, and a list that names the asset without a
usable hash is an error such as `lists <file>, but with no sha256,
sha512, blake3, sha1 or md5 hash` or `lists <file> more than once with
different hashes`. A `checksum` option or a `mise.lock` entry, including
an additional asset's entry, takes over in that case.
- **Windows hash tool output**: a per-asset checksum file written by
certutil or PowerShell's `Get-FileHash` (ripgrep and deno ship these for
Windows) is read by taking its one standalone hash. A file with no hash
or two different hashes is still an error.
- **Large lists**: checksum lists were split into copies of every field,
so a very large list used memory many times its size. Lists are now
parsed line by line without copying, including the Erlang, Elixir and
`mise version` parsers.

**Which release is installed**

- **Release for another tag**: the GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo release
lookups took whatever release the host or a mirror answered with. A
release whose tag is not the one requested is now refused:

  ```
refusing GitHub release <tag>: the API was asked for
<owner>/<repo>@<requested>; check the host `url_replacements` sends
api.github.com to
  ```

For a registry tool, the attestation requirement is now judged on both
the requested and the resolved version.

- **`minimum_release_age` and twin tags**: the cutoff picked a version
by one tag spelling, but the asset lookup tried every spelling, so a
newer release published under the other one could be installed. A
version the cutoff chose is now installed only from a release older than
the cutoff; if mise finds only a newer one, the install fails:

  ```
refusing to install <tool>@<version>: minimum_release_age chose
<version> by a release older than the cutoff, but the only release of it
mise found is newer: <reason>. Install it by naming the version exactly
(<tool>@<version>), or wait until the release is older than
minimum_release_age.
  ```

  Versions from `mise.lock` or named exactly are not affected.

**Lockfile digests**

- **md5 and sha1**: when a release offered both an md5 or sha1 file and
a sha256 list, the first one found was used and recorded in `mise.lock`,
and `mise lock` kept reusing it. mise now uses md5 or sha1 only when no
list gives a stronger hash, and then records a sha256 or blake3 digest
of the file. `mise lock` checks the file against an existing md5 or sha1
entry as well as the new hash, and replaces the entry with sha256.

**Registry attestations**

- **Numeric versions past `attestations_since`**: only three-part semver
versions were compared with a registry tool's `attestations_since`, so a
release tagged `v0.72` past a `0.71.1` boundary installed without an
attestation. A version made only of dot-separated numbers is now
compared by those numbers, a missing one counting as 0. Channels, refs
and pre-releases such as `nightly` or `2.50-1` are still exempt.

**Docs**

- The github backend page says which checksum list formats mise reads,
when a missing or unreadable list fails the install, and how md5 and
sha1 lists are recorded. The security page explains twin tags under
`minimum_release_age`. The registry contributing guide, the aqua backend
page, the paranoid page and the registry schema describe which versions
`attestations_since` covers.

## Compatibility

- An install now fails when a release's only checksum file cannot be
downloaded (including during an outage) or lists the asset without a
hash mise can read. Pin the asset with the `checksum` option or a
`mise.lock` entry to install anyway. This PR fails closed; the
alternative is to install unchecked with a warning.
- A `minimum_release_age` install whose only matching release is newer
than the cutoff now fails; naming the version exactly installs it. This
PR fails; the alternative is to fall back to the newer release.
- `mise.lock` entries can change on the next `mise lock`: md5 and sha1
entries become sha256, and a release that publishes a sha512 list
(caddy, for one) is now recorded as sha512 where a sha256 was recorded
before. Teammates on older and newer mise may see these entries change
back and forth.
- A per-asset checksum file holding a single `<hash> <other-name>` line
now gives its hash instead of failing; a wrong hash still fails at
download.
- A registry tool release tagged with two or four numbers at or past
`attestations_since` now needs an attestation, as three-part tags
already did.

## Validation

Each fix has unit tests that were seen failing without it, including
fixtures copied byte for byte from ripgrep's and deno's Windows checksum
files. Locking 76 real `github:` tools for linux-x64, macos-arm64 and
windows-x64 with and without this PR: 74 gave the same result, atuin now
locks for Linux and macOS where it failed before, and caddy moves from
sha256 to sha512. An install on Windows was not run, and the
`minimum_release_age` twin-tag case was tested for GitLab and Forgejo
but not GitHub.
