fix(wrappers): put the wrapper directory first on PATH for mise x, tasks and mise env (#16070)

A [command
wrapper](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html#command-wrappers) was
skipped by commands that a child process looked up, when the directory
holding the real command is listed before mise's shims on `PATH`. The
usual case is rustup's `~/.cargo/bin`:

```sh
# ~/.zshenv
export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$HOME/.local/share/mise/shims:$PATH"
```

```toml
# mise.toml
[wrappers.cargo]
command = "mbx"
env = { MBX_CARGO_SHIM_MODE = "1" }
```

`mise x -- cargo build` ran `mbx`, but a `cargo` started by anything
underneath mise did not:

```sh
mise x -- sh -c 'command -v cargo'
# before: ~/.cargo/bin/cargo
# after:  ~/.local/share/mise/command-wrappers/bin/cargo
```

The same held for a task's script (`run = "cargo check"`), a build tool
or agent that calls `cargo` itself, and a shell that evaluates `mise
env`. Every one of those builds went around the wrapper with no warning.

## What changes

The wrapper directory is now the first entry of the `PATH` a project's
commands run with (`mise x`, tasks, `mise env` and shim dispatches),
whenever the config has a wrapper. That matches an activated shell and
`mise activate --shims`, which already put it first, and the lookup
`mise x` does for the program it starts.

A task's own `_.path` directories go behind the wrapper directory too.
Before, they got ahead of it when the inherited `PATH` had no shims
directory, so a `cargo` in a task's `_.path` skipped the wrapper.

What stays as it was:

- Directories listed before the shims still come ahead of the tools mise
adds, so a `node` you put first on purpose still wins over a
mise-installed one.
- All projects share one wrapper directory, so it can hold a shim that
another project's wrapper left for a command this project does not wrap.
Such a shim does nothing here. A child's lookup of `node` runs the next
`node` on its `PATH` (a directory you list before the shims, a task's
`_.path`, a mise tool), whether the shim was run by name or by the path
a lookup returned. That `node` gets the arguments and the environment
the shim was given, so inside a task it keeps the task's `_.path` and
env, and the shim does not run `auto_update` for a mise tool named
`node`. A real command in a shared
[`shims_dir`](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration/settings.html#shims_dir)
such as `~/.local/bin` counts as the next `node` too: only a file that
is a mise shim is treated as one. `mise x -- node` leaves the shim out
of its lookup and looks mise's tools up first, as it did. Not covered:
Windows `exe` and `file` shims run the command with `mise x`, so mise's
tools come first there. And PowerShell starts a shim by the path of the
file it found, not by the name typed, so `node.exe` typed there runs
what `node` does.
- Installs and `postinstall` hooks keep the `PATH` order they had. A
wrapper directory inherited from the shell stays behind the tool's own
directories there.
- With no wrapper configured, mise does not add the wrapper directory,
and a copy that is only inherited keeps its place.

This is not specific to Rust. Any wrapped command whose real binary sits
in a directory listed before the shims was affected. Rust shows it most
because mise-managed Rust also uses `~/.cargo/bin`, which is outside
mise's installs directory and so keeps its inherited position.

## Why it happened

mise keeps inherited `PATH` entries that precede its shims directory
ahead of everything it adds, and it added the wrapper directory the same
way as a tool directory. The `PATH` mise builds for a project's commands
now puts the wrapper directory first; the `PATH` it builds for installs
and hooks is built as before.

## Validation

- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_command_wrappers_inherited_path`: fails on
the released 2026.11.11 binary at `mise x -- sh -c 'command -v cargo'`,
passes with this change. It covers `mise x`, a child shell, `mise env`,
task scripts, a task's `_.path` with and without a shims directory, the
unchanged order for tools, a wrapper shim left by another project (run
by name, by path, with `activate_aggressive`, from a task with `_.path`,
and with an unchanged environment), a `postinstall` hook, and the
no-wrapper case.
- New e2e test
`e2e/cli/test_command_wrappers_leftover_shim_auto_update`: a shim
another project left passes the command on without running a due
`auto_update`, and the tool's own shim still updates it.
- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_command_wrappers_shared_shims_dir`: with
`shims_dir` shared with other commands, a leftover wrapper shim passes
on to a real command in that directory, and a mise shim there still
resolves its tool.
- `e2e-win/command_wrappers.Tests.ps1` now also runs `mise x --
WrapTool` against `[wrappers.wraptool]`: Windows command names ignore
case. A new hardlink-mode case runs a wrapper shim another project left
for `greet`: by its path with a `greet.cmd` next on `PATH`, as `greet`
and as `greet.exe` with a `greet.exe` behind that batch file (`greet`
runs the batch file, `greet.exe` the `.exe`, which receives the `PATH`
the shim was started with), then by name with a `mise generate
task-stubs --windows-launcher exe` launcher for a task of that name. It
found three Windows gaps, all fixed: a shim run by name looked for a
file named `greet` and not `greet.exe`, so it never passed the command
on; a shim run by its path looked for `greet.exe` only, so it missed a
`greet.cmd`; and the launcher, which is the same executable as an `exe`
shim, was taken for a tool shim.
- New `path_env` unit tests for the order, for `PATH`s that do not lead
with wrappers, and for adding to a `PATH` mise already built.
- Existing e2e tests around wrappers, `mise x` PATH order, shims and
`_.path` pass locally.

The command wrappers docs state the order and the rules above.

security: refuse terminal input injection in sandboxes, verify OCI base layers and bound LSP work (#16073)

The Linux sandbox, `mise oci build` and the language server each had a
gap:

- a sandboxed command could type input into the terminal, which the
user's shell ran after the command exited;
- under `--deny-net` alone, a command could get a socket from a process
outside the sandbox by attaching to it;
- `mise oci build` reused a base layer from `./mise-oci` without hashing
it, accepted a tag where an index must name a digest, sent netrc logins
to the token host a registry named, unpacked the base image as root into
a directory other users could enter, and followed base-image symlinks
while preparing apt;
- the language server could read a `/proc` file without end, and its
task-cycle check could take tens of seconds or gigabytes on a large
`mise.toml`.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

- **Terminal input in sandboxes (Linux)**: the `TIOCSTI` and `TIOCLINUX`
ioctls, which push input into a terminal, now fail with `Operation not
permitted` under any file, network or process restriction. Before,
`/dev/tty` was writable in every sandbox and nothing refused them, so on
kernels that still allow `TIOCSTI` a command could type a command into
the user's shell. The seccomp filter that refuses them is now installed
for file restrictions too, not only for `--deny-net` and process
restrictions. Other ioctls, such as reading the window size, still work.
- **`--deny-net` (Linux 6.7 and later)**: the command now also runs in a
Landlock domain that refuses TCP bind and connect; with a file
restriction, it is the same domain as those restrictions, and without
one it refuses nothing on the filesystem. A process in a domain cannot
ptrace or read the memory of a process outside it, so it can no longer
have one of them open a socket and hand it over. Files, exec, renames,
hard links and `AF_UNIX` sockets work as before, including inside an
outer Landlock sandbox.
- **Base layers already in the OCI layout**: `mise oci build` skipped
downloading a base layer when a file named after its digest was in the
output directory (`./mise-oci` by default, which a repository can ship),
and never hashed it. A layer is now reused only when it is a regular
file that hashes to its digest; anything else at that path, a symlink
included, is replaced with the downloaded bytes and mise warns
`replacing <path>: its content does not match its digest`.
- **Manifest index entries**: the manifest an index lists for the
platform must be named by a `sha256` digest, and the manifest fetched
under it is checked against that digest. Before, an entry holding a tag
was fetched as a tag, unverified, even when the index itself was pinned
by digest. This applies to `mise oci build` base images and to OCI task
files.
- **Registry token requests**: after a Bearer challenge, the token
request to the registry's `realm` goes out with only the registry login
mise was given, or none. Before, it went through the client that adds
netrc logins, so the netrc login for whatever host the realm named was
sent there. Transient failures are still retried.
- **System package rootfs**: `mise oci build` unpacks the base image for
apt and apk installs into a temporary directory with mode `0700`.
Before, it had the umask's mode (usually `0755`), so other local users
could reach the image's set-uid programs and files while the root build
ran. The configuration staged by `mise bootstrap --adopt --dry-run`,
which holds decrypted files, is now in a `0700` directory too.
- **apt preparation**: rewriting `etc/apt` and creating dpkg's status
file and apt's state directories now refuse a symlink anywhere below the
rootfs, with `refusing to follow symlink component <path>`. Before, a
base image whose `etc`, `etc/apt` or `var/lib/dpkg` was a symlink made
those writes land on the build host as root.
- **Language server file reads**: config and task include files are read
up to the 1 MiB limit and skipped past it. Before, the size check used
the size the file system reported, so a `mise.local.toml` or include
linked to a `/proc` file (which reports 0 bytes) was read without end.
- **Language server cycle check**: `task-cycle` now finds groups of
tasks that depend on each other in one pass and searches for cycles only
inside them, with a fixed work limit per file. A file past the limit
gets the first cycle diagnostics in file order, the same ones each time.
Only the first 100 unknown task names in a file get a "did you mean"
suggestion.

## Compatibility

- On x86_64, a 32-bit x86 program no longer runs under `--deny-write`,
`--deny-read` or other file-only restrictions, because the seccomp
filter stops system calls made through another architecture's ABI. It

security(backend): verify native cargo binaries and bound what cargo and spm read from packages (#16077)

With `cargo.binstall_native = true`, mise installs a crate's prebuilt
binary itself, following the crate's `[package.metadata.binstall]`
table. It did not check the downloaded crate against crates.io's
checksum, ignored the crate's minisign key, fetched binaries over any
URL scheme, and used crates.io even when Cargo was set up for another
registry. The `spm` backend had related gaps: `core:spm:<url>` skipped
the trust prompt for self-hosted forges, GitLab was picked when
`gitlab.com` appeared anywhere in the name, and per-platform `api_url`
values shared one version cache entry.

This PR closes those, and bounds what both backends read from a
downloaded package: metadata files, template expansion, `cfg()` nesting,
total unpacked size and repeated executables.

## What changes

**Native cargo installs (`cargo.binstall_native`)**

- **Crate checksum**: the `.crate` mise downloads to read
`[package.metadata.binstall]` was not checked, so whoever served the
download chose the binary URL. It is now checked against the sha256
crates.io publishes before it is unpacked. On a mismatch mise builds
with `cargo install`, which checks the same checksum.
- **Minisign signatures**: a crate's
`[package.metadata.binstall.signing]` table was ignored. When a crate
declares a minisign key, mise now downloads the signature (from the
`file` template, `{ url }.sig` by default, https only) and verifies each
binary before unpacking it, hashing it in chunks so the binary is never
read into memory whole. A binary that does not verify is not installed:
mise warns `not using native cargo binary artifact <url>: <reason>` and
runs `cargo install`. A malformed `signing` table or an algorithm other
than minisign is an error, not "unsigned".
- **https only**: the binary URL expanded from `pkg-url` was fetched
whatever its scheme. A URL that is not `https` now fails with `native
cargo binary <kind> must be downloaded over https: <url>`, and mise
builds the crate from source.
- **Other registries**: the native installer read crates.io whenever
`cargo.registry_name` was unset, while `cargo install` honoured Cargo's
own `registry.default`, `CARGO_REGISTRY_DEFAULT` or a
`[source.crates-io]` replacement. mise now reads `$CARGO_HOME` and the
`.cargo` config files that `cargo install` would use, and skips the
native installer when they name another registry or cannot be read.
- **Template expansion**: `pkg-url` placeholders were replaced key by
key over the whole string, so a substituted value could be expanded
again and grow without bound. Expansion is now a single pass, and a
result over 8 KiB fails with `native cargo binary template expands to
more than 8192 bytes`.
- **Total unpacked size**: a crate that names several binaries gets one
archive per binary, and each had its own `extract_max_ratio` allowance
with no total. All of a crate's archives are now held to one limit, the
limit of a single archive of their combined size.
- **`cfg()` overrides**: an override key nested thousands of `not()`,
`all()` or `any()` levels deep overflowed the stack and aborted `mise
install`. A key nested more than 32 levels deep is now ignored as a
whole, with a debug line.

**`spm` backend**

- **Trust for `core:spm:`**: `spm:<self-hosted url>` already needed
`mise trust`, because mise sends the forge token to that host, but the
same key spelled `core:spm:<url>` did not. Keys are now checked after
leading `core:` prefixes are removed, in `mise.toml` and
`.tool-versions`. github.com and gitlab.com stay trust-free.
- **GitLab detection**: GitLab was chosen when `gitlab.com` appeared
anywhere in the tool name, so `spm:acme/gitlab.com-sync` was listed from
gitlab.com and a GitHub Enterprise URL could get `GITLAB_TOKEN`. Only
the URL's host is compared now.
- **Version cache**: the version list cache ignored per-platform
`provider`, `api_url` and `artifactbundle_asset` values, so a list
fetched for one `api_url` was served for another. Those values are now
part of the cache key.
- **Repeated executables**: an artifact bundle's `info.json` can list
one file under many names, and each name was copied in full. Each file
is now copied once into the install, and every name in `bin/` links to
that copy. Choosing which executables to install now also takes linear
time in the number of names.
- **Refused bundles in mise.lock**: when an artifact bundle was refused
after its URL and checksum were recorded (for example an `info.json`
over the limit) and mise fell back to a source build, mise.lock still
pinned the refused bundle. The earlier lock entry is now put back.

**Both backends**

- **Package metadata**: a crate's `Cargo.toml` and an artifact bundle's
`info.json` were read whole, and the crate's manifest could be read
through a link the crate shipped. Both are now read only when they are
regular files of at most 1 MiB (`not reading <path>: it is larger than 1
MiB, the most mise reads from a downloaded package's metadata`), and a
crate with a link that leaves it is refused. Cargo then builds from
source; spm builds from source unless a bundle is required.

**Docs**

- The cargo backend page says when mise skips the native installer, that
a crate's `pkg-url` must be https (a `url_replacements` rule that
rewrites it to http still downloads over http), and that a binary whose
minisign signature does not verify is not installed.

## Compatibility

- With `cargo.binstall_native`, a crate whose binary URL is `http://`,
whose declared minisign signature is missing or does not verify, or
whose crate fails its checksum is now built with `cargo install`. This
PR falls back to building from source; the alternative is to make a
failed check abort the install.
- A crate whose binaries carry a legacy (not prehashed) minisign
signature does not verify, so it is built with `cargo install` too.
- An `http://` repository URL is refused, not upgraded, even when a
`url_replacements` entry would rewrite it to https. This PR refuses; the
alternative is to upgrade `http://` to `https://` before the check.
- If your Cargo config names another registry or replaces the crates.io
source, `cargo.binstall_native` no longer installs prebuilt binaries for
you; mise runs `cargo install`.
- Untrusted configs with `core:spm:https://<self-hosted>/…` keys now ask
for `mise trust`, like `spm:` keys already did.
- A self-hosted GitLab whose host only contains `gitlab.com` needs
`provider = "gitlab"`, which the docs already require.
- Multi-binary crates whose archives unpack to more than the combined
limit need a higher `extract_max_ratio`, and executables an spm bundle
lists under several names are now links to one copy.

## Validation

Each fix has unit tests, and all but the linear-time spm change were
seen failing without their fix; the signature test checks a real
minisign signature and refuses tampered and unsigned binaries. Comparing
builds with and without this PR: `core:spm:` with a self-hosted URL now
asks for trust, `spm:acme/gitlab.com-sync` is listed from GitHub, and a
native install of `cargo:cargo-binstall` downloaded and verified its
real signature. A failing checksum or signature was tested only in unit
tests, and no e2e test was added.

security(packslip): pin signing keys by fingerprint and stop project config waiving stampers in safe mode (#16085)

Several parts of the `packslip:` backend and `mise skills sync` trusted
more than they should have:

- a pin held to a signing key's ID, which is only text in the key line,
so a different key carrying the same ID passed;
- a pin for a GitHub or GitLab repository was keyed by the exact
spelling of its name, so the same repository in other letter case
started without one;
- a release list kept across commands could be confirmed by the vendor's
host long after a newer list had withdrawn a release;
- in safe mode, a repository's own config could set `trust = "vendor"`
and so waive the `packslip.stampers` you require;
- `mise skills sync` wrote its exclude block through a symlinked or
redirected `.git`, and a repository skill fetch had no limit on how many
entries its listings could name;
- release lists, stamp lists and manifests could be gigabytes before
anything verified them, and `mise hook-env` could take minutes on a
release with many resources.

This PR fixes each of those.

## What changes

- **Signing key pins**: `pins.toml` now records the fingerprint of the
whole public key that signed the last accepted release of a key-signed
project, not only its ID. A release signed by another key that carries
the same ID is refused:

  ```
is signed by another key that carries the ID <id> (fingerprint
<fingerprint>), but the key with fingerprint <pinned> signed what mise
accepted before
  ```

The message also names `mise packslip forget`. A pin written before this
change holds by ID and gains the fingerprint from the next release
accepted. `mise.lock` still records the key ID only.
- **Repository names in other letter case**: pins, release-list
sequences, stamp-list sequences, `mise packslip forget` and, in safe
mode, a global `trust = "vendor"` entry now treat a `github.com` or
`gitlab.com` repository name as the same project in any letter case, as
the forge does. Before, `github.com/O/R` had no pin even when
`github.com/o/r` did. A monorepo subpath and a name on any other host
still compare exactly. Pins stored under two spellings become one on the
next accepted install.
- **Release lists are read whole on every command**: mise no longer
keeps a copy of a vendor's release list with its `ETag` or
`Last-Modified` to send a conditional request next time. Before, a `304
Not Modified` reused the stored copy, so an older list once answered
under the current list's validator would keep being confirmed and a
withdrawn release would stay installable. Copies stored by earlier
versions are no longer read.
- **Paranoid provenance and "no release list"**: with the `provenance`
category of `paranoid` enabled, an answer from mise-versions that a
project has no release list is now checked with GitHub. A list found
there is verified and applied, only a `404` answer confirms there is
none, and a timeout, a refused connection or any other failure to read
GitHub fails the command. Normal mode is unchanged.
- **`trust = "vendor"` in safe mode**: safe mode now honours `trust =
"vendor"` only when a `[tools]` entry of global or system config sets it
for the same project. Before, a repository's `mise.toml`,
`.tool-versions`, task tools or monorepo subproject could set it and
install a release that none of your `packslip.stampers` listed. The
refusal now says where to put the option:

  ```
packslip:<project>@<version> carries no stamp from <hosts>; mise
installs only versions a trusted stamper lists. Set `trust = "vendor"`
in the tool's `[tools]` entry in global config to take the vendor's own
manifest instead
  ```

An ignored setting is logged at debug level: `packslip:<project>:
ignoring trust = "vendor": global config does not set it for this tool
and safe mode (MISE_SAFE=1) is on`.
- **`mise skills sync` exclude block**: the block is written only into a
real `.git` directory, or into a submodule's directory under an
enclosing repository's `.git/modules`. A `.git` that is a symbolic link
or a `gitdir:` file naming any other directory is left alone. If
`.git/info`, `.git/info/exclude` or its `exclude.mise-lock` file is a
link, sync refuses with `<path> is a link`.
- **Repository skill size**: fetching a skill from a repository stops
once its directory listings name more than 1024 entries, files and
subdirectories together, and the skill is not installed. Before, the
listings could keep the fetch going for as long as they kept answering.
- **Size of release lists, stamp lists and manifests**: a release list
or stamp list is read up to 4 MiB, and a manifest read while resolving a
version is held to the same 4 MiB as one read at install. A larger
mirror copy is not used and GitHub is asked instead; a larger answer
from the host fails with `is larger than 4.0 MiB`. Before, only the
general 128 MiB download limit applied, so a `[tools]` entry could make
`mise ls` or `mise lock` use several GiB of memory.
- **Shell completions of a large release**: `mise hook-env` now groups a
release's resources by executable once, instead of once for each
executable. Before, a release with many executables and resources could
make every prompt take seconds or minutes.

The packslip crate requirement is raised to 1.11.3.

## Compatibility

- Release lists are downloaded in full on every command that needs one,
instead of being revalidated. This PR does that; the alternative is to
keep the conditional request and bind each stored copy to a digest of
its text, which saves bandwidth for large lists but needs a new cache
format. Old copies under the cache directory are left on disk and can be
deleted with `mise cache clear`.
- With `paranoid` `provenance`, a project without a release list costs
one extra request to GitHub, and the command fails when GitHub cannot be
reached or rate-limits it. Set `GITHUB_TOKEN` to avoid the rate limit.
- In safe mode, `trust = "vendor"` set in a project's `mise.toml`,
`.tool-versions`, a task's tools, a monorepo subproject, or on the
command line no longer waives `packslip.stampers`. Move the option into
the tool's `[tools]` entry in global config. A global `[tool_alias]`
does not count either.
- A repository whose `.git` is a symlink or names another directory (for
example one made with `git init --separate-git-dir`) no longer gets the
exclude block, so its skill links show in `git status`. Add them to
`.gitignore` yourself.
- A skill directory with more than 1024 entries, or a release list,
stamp list or manifest larger than 4 MiB, is refused.
- The first key-signed install after upgrading records the key's
fingerprint in `pins.toml`. A vendor that later rotates to a new key
with the same ID is refused until you run `mise packslip forget`.

## Validation

Each fix has unit tests, including a release signed by a second key with
a copied ID, a pin looked up under another letter case, a host that
would confirm an older list, oversized lists and manifests, endless
directory listings and links in place of the exclude file. New e2e tests
cover paranoid release lists and safe-mode stamper requirements. Those
two e2e tests and the existing `mise skills sync` exclude e2e test pass.
Not verified: the e2e tests against a build without these fixes, and the
speed of `mise hook-env` in an optimised build.

perf(lockfile): cache a lockfile's parsed entries instead of its TOML table (#16095)

Every mise command reads `mise.lock`, and for a project locked for
several platforms that read was about an eighth of `mise hook-env`, the
command that runs on every shell prompt. mise already kept the parsed
TOML of a large lockfile in its cache directory, but each command still
turned that generic table back into lockfile entries: it rebuilt every
table and string, then checked and converted each of the entries (261
platform entries in a 29-tool project locked for nine platforms).

mise now caches the entries themselves, so a command reads them back
directly.

What a command does with a lockfile is unchanged:

- The cache holds only what the lockfile's text says on its own.
Everything that depends on where the file is, on settings or on the
registry still runs on every read: sidecar paths, backend names, the
"names no tool; ignoring the entry" warning, and the checks that an
entry fits the lockfile's revision.
- The cache file is named by a hash of the lockfile's text and by the
mise build, so any edit to the lockfile, or another mise, parses the
text again. Only a lockfile that parsed without error is cached, so an
error is reported on every read.
- An entry with an npm or Python dependency graph is cached as its
parsed TOML and converted on each read, as before.
- A cache file that cannot be read is ignored and rewritten.
- A lockfile under 4 KB is not cached, as before.

One difference: when a lockfile has two separate errors, which one is
reported first can change, because every entry is now converted before
the first sidecar path is resolved.

The cache files have a new name, so the first command after upgrading
parses each lockfile once.

## Measured

Release builds linked as releases are, in the 29-tool project the
`*-large` benchmarks use (a 77 KB `mise.lock`). Both sides were built
before #16051 merged: "before" is `main` at f6f8e6dd5c, "this PR" is

mise no longer reports installs. After installing a core or registry
tool, mise used to send a beacon to `mise-versions.jdx.dev/t` with the
tool, its backend, the version, the OS and the architecture. That
request is gone: mise now contacts a server only to fetch something the

accepted so a config shared with mise 2026.11.14 or older can keep
`use_versions_host_track = false` to opt those releases out. With a
deprecation warning, users would be told to delete the setting, and
deleting it would turn the beacon back on in their older mise releases.

### Docs

A new FAQ entry, [Does mise phone
home?](https://mise.jdx.dev/faq.html#does-mise-phone-home), lists every
request mise makes to jdx.dev hosts and which settings turn them off:

- version lists and GitHub release data from mise-versions, Java's build
catalog from mise-java, and precompiled Python's index from
mise-versions (which `use_versions_host = false` does not turn off)
- the daily check for a newer mise

The `use_versions_host` docs no longer list install counts among what
the host's logs are used for.

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`
passes.
- The `versions_host` unit tests pass, along with e2e
`cli/test_settings_ls`.

been removed, along with the e2e harness's


That PR was meant to make only `system_packages.elevate_with`

Fixes #16068

trusted project's value is read without the warning.

fix(cron): show job notices when the owner conversation's model cannot run (#207186)

## Problem

Cron's fixed notices reach the owner conversation only as a session-event model turn. These are the auto-disabled notice (including `account-unavailable` from #207097) and the failure alert when no direct transport delivers it, which also covers repair fallbacks and the #207091 reset alert. The notice text becomes the turn's input row. When the conversation's own model cannot run, for example on the same signed-out account, the turn fails before it starts and writes no row. The user never sees why their automation stopped.

## Fix

The Gateway cron adapter (`src/gateway/server-cron-targets.ts`) keeps the notice turn, because it is also the agent's repair turn (#188105). When a job notice's turn settles `failed` without starting and is not retained for retry, the adapter posts the same text through the existing session notice writer (`postSessionNotice`). This writes one transcript row, sends it to the conversation's channel unless the event is private, and adds the text to the next turn's context. No model turn is involved.

- It uses the captured target's store path and `deliver` policy.
- When the model works, nothing changes: the user sees the same row and the agent's reply.

## Review

Fable reviewed this adversarially. Applied: drop the extra flag (`jobId` already identifies job notices); skip retryable outcomes, because the retained event still owns its text; honor the captured target's `deliver` and store path.

Not applied:
- A re-check of requester authority before the post. Authority is decided once, when the turn target is captured. Repo rules forbid `assertCurrent()`-style re-checks.
- Always posting notices directly and hiding the repair input. That would change what users see when the model works, and would send a second channel message.

Accepted edge cases:
- A notice whose turn is `cancelled` by restart or supersession is not reposted.
- A session that does not exist yet (`createIfMissing`) and fails before creation has nowhere to post. The warning is logged.

## Evidence

- `src/gateway/server-cron-notice-delivery.test.ts` uses a real Gateway target resolver, a real session-event handoff and an owner model with no usable account. On the merge base, 0 visible notices. On this branch, exactly 1.
- Cron failure-alert, delivery-outcome, startup-notification, Gateway notification and failure-repair final-effect suites pass.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

fix: keep recovery prompts out of Claude chat history (#207128)

Root cause: src/agents/cli-runner/execute-plugin.ts:481 marks CLI input as host-generated only from the run's input provenance, but the stranded-reply retry (src/auto-reply/reply/stranded-reply-recovery.ts:56-89) correctly keeps the human turn's provenance, so Claude Code saves the retry prompt as a plain user row and chat.history shows it as the operator's own message.

Fixes #206304

Thanks @fray-ai for the report and the precise code trace, and @Tosko4 for the first fix in this PR.

## What Problem This Solves

With a `claude-cli` agent and `messages.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`, a turn that ends with plain text queues the stranded-reply retry (`[System] Your previous reply was not delivered ...`). That retry reached Claude Code as ordinary user input, Claude stored it as a normal user row, and the Control UI drew it as a right-aligned operator bubble.

## User Impact

The retry no longer appears as a message the operator wrote. The delivered reply still arrives. An operator who types the same `[System] ...` text still sees it as their own message, and existing history is not rewritten. Nothing changes for the embedded runtime or for permissions.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The CLI candidate sets `promptOrigin: "host"` from the existing `FollowupRun.strandedReplyRetry` flag (`agent-runner-cli-candidate.ts`). `RunCliAgentParams` carries that one optional field, with the same value type `CliBackendExecuteContext.promptOrigin` already uses.
- The plugin CLI runner marks host input when that field is set or when the provenance is host-generated, as before (`execute-plugin.ts`). The Claude backend then sends `isSynthetic: true`, Claude saves an `isMeta` row, and the existing history import skips it.
- The retry's `inputProvenance` is unchanged (`external_user`). The first version of this PR switched it to `internal_system`; that value feeds requester-profile, continuation, collaborative-steering and personal-MCP requester checks (`reply-tool-authority.ts:353`, `reply-tool-authority-inbound.ts:83/116/214`, `agent-bundle-mcp-webchat-requester.ts:42`), reply threading and model urgency. Those changes are reverted, together with the `missingReplyNoticeAllowed` change it needed.
- No text classification: an operator who types the same `[System] ...` text still sees their own bubble. Existing history is not rewritten.

Production: +9/-1 lines in 3 files. Tests: one regression at the CLI dispatch boundary (+18); the PR's other tests are dropped.

## Evidence

Built Gateway + Control UI from `450c4b640ed6` (main) and this head in a secretless node:24.22.1 container. Agent `main` runs on `claude-cli` with a stand-in `claude` that writes a real Claude Code project JSONL (synthetic input -> `isMeta`) and calls the real OpenClaw MCP `message` tool; agent `embedded` runs on the OpenClaw runtime with a scripted model. Real Chromium (Playwright 1.64.1) drives WebChat sessions. Screenshots and the full table: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/207128#issuecomment-7232846921

| case | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| claude-cli stranded once: operator bubble with retry text (live / reload) | 1 / 1 | 0 / 0 |
| same: delivered reply "Delivered answer P206304." | shown | shown |
| same: chat.history retry row | `role: user`, no provenance, importedFrom claude-cli | absent (meta row skipped) |
| Claude stdin for retry | `isSynthetic` absent | `isSynthetic: true` |
| control: operator types the identical `[System] ...` text | own bubble, `external_user` | own bubble, `external_user` |
| control: retry also ends with plain text (second miss) | retry shown as operator bubble; retry final shown; no "No answer" notice | no operator bubble; retry final shown; no "No answer" notice (same as main) |
| control: embedded (non-CLI) agent, stranded once | no retry bubble, delivered | identical |

Regression test `agent-runner-execution-cli-sessions.test.ts` "sends a stranded-reply retry as host input without changing its provenance (#206304)": fails with the candidate line removed (`- "promptOrigin": "host"`), passes at head.

## Merge danger

Two-way door: no stored state, schema, config or protocol change; a revert fully restores the old behavior. Blast radius: only stranded-reply retries on plugin CLI backends (Claude CLI) change their native input marker.

ci: check the Plugin SDK export surface on every pull request (#207167)

## Problem

#206995 added a Plugin SDK export without a surface budget line and merged with green PR CI. Main's SDK surface check then failed (`public exports 3933 > 3932`, `public callable exports 2260 > 2259`) until a follow-up added the line.

Why PR CI did not catch it:
- `check:changed` selects `plugin-sdk:check-exports` and `plugin-sdk:surface:check` for SDK paths. But PR CI calls it lint-only (`ci.yml`, "Run changed lint", `lintOnly: true`), so only lint commands run.
- The only other runner is the `generated-doc-baselines` job in `workflow-sanity.yml`. It runs only on `workflow_dispatch`, never on a pull request.

## Fix

The baseline-ratchets job (`scripts/ci-baseline-ratchets.mts`) already runs on every node PR. It now also runs `plugin-sdk:check-exports` and `plugin-sdk:surface:check` on every run:
- The surface check is a large TypeScript program, so it runs in the same slot as the database-worker and database-dialect snapshots. They run one after another and never overlap (the memory rule from `c695d653`). The export check is light and joins the shared queue.
- It runs on every PR, not only SDK-path PRs: the SDK import closure reaches far outside `src/plugin-sdk`. For example, adding `@deprecated` to `src/channels/chat-type.ts` moves the deprecated-export count, and no changed-path rule sees that.

No new workflow or job.

## Impact

Contributors: a PR that changes the SDK export surface without its budget line now fails `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets` instead of turning main red after merge. Cost per PR: one surface check (about 7 s and 3.5 GB peak locally) in the existing job.

## Evidence

- Red/green on a PR-like change set: a scratch copy of main with #206995's export added on top of a tagged base, run with `pnpm check:baseline-ratchets --base <base> --no-merge-base`:
  - a new SDK function without a budget line: `plugin-sdk-surface` fails, `public exports 3933 > 3932`, `public callable exports 2261 > 2260`, exit 1;
  - the same change plus the budget lines: `[ok] plugin-sdk-exports`, `[ok] plugin-sdk-surface`, exit 0.
- `test/scripts/ci-baseline-ratchets.test.ts`: the expected command list now includes both SDK checks in their slots (4/4).
- Adversarial review: a first version selected the checks by changed path. The review showed that version missed real budget inputs outside `src/plugin-sdk` and reproduced a miss. This version drops path selection.
- Local review on this head: patch is correct, 0 findings.
- CI cost on this PR's runner: `plugin-sdk-surface` 8.48 s and `plugin-sdk-exports` 0.28 s inside `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets`, which took 4m50s in total.

fix: auto-disable automations whose account was signed out (#207097)

## What Problem This Solves

When the account an automation was recorded with is removed or signed out, every run of that automation fails. A recurring automation then fails again on every scheduled run, indefinitely: the refusal is classified as `unknown`, and nothing ends the loop. On one production deployment, 11 automations on one signed-out account failed 270 times in 2.8 days. 170 of those were `All models failed (4)`, because every configured fallback was on the same signed-out account. Six of them were still looping when measured.

## User Impact

An automation whose recorded account was removed, signed out or replaced is now auto-disabled after the first run that nothing else could finish. It uses the existing auto-disable mechanism with a new reason, `account-unavailable`. The owner gets one notice that names the repair:
1. sign in again (`openclaw models auth login --provider <provider> --force`);
2. record the account (`openclaw automations edit <id> --model <provider/model>@<profileId>`, or a plain model to use a configured key);
3. run `openclaw automations enable <id>`.

`openclaw automations list` shows the job as `disabled (account)`, and `openclaw doctor` lists the recorded reason. The notice does not name the account; run history keeps the full refusal.

The job keeps running when:
- a fallback on another provider finishes the run (the run stays `ok`);
- a fallback failed for a reason that can pass, for example a 429 (normal retry schedule);
- the account store was only briefly interrupted, for example by a state database lifecycle change.

A forced manual run that preserves a scheduled one-shot occurrence leaves that occurrence alone.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix is at the owners that already exist:
- **Producer.** `acquireCronInferenceAuthorization` gives its refusal a code when the recorded account is gone or was replaced. The original `AuthProfileAuthorizationError` stays as `cause`. The code is added only when the authorization owner reports that the profile itself is absent, retired or expired: a new `accountGone` fact on `AuthProfileAuthorizationError`. Other retirements keep their old behavior.
- **Run inference.** It marks the refusal when a fallback candidate on another provider runs. From then on the recorded account was not the run's only way to execute.
- **Classifier.** `resolveCronConfigurationRefusal` classifies the refusal on both run paths (isolated and session target), and only when nothing else could run the job: either a surfaced refusal that no other provider bypassed, or a fallback summary whose every attempt was that refusal. It never matches error text.
- **Outcome.** `applyJobResult` calls the existing `autoDisableCronJob` once, with reason `account-unavailable` and the existing `auto-disabled` notification in place of the failure alert. Aborted and restart-interrupted runs never disable. The permanent-disable branch for plugin and operator-source jobs leaves this refusal to the auto-disable path.
- **Readers.** The new value is added to the Gateway protocol's `autoDisabled.reason` union, the Doctor reader, the CLI status label, and the Control UI sidebar's shape check, so such a job stays in the attention list.

**Downgrade check** (stable `v2026.11.10`, isolated state, host variables stripped). A store holding one job with `autoDisabled.reason: "account-unavailable"` and one ordinary job loads exactly like a control store holding `schedule-errors`:
- the list shows all jobs, and the new job reads as `disabled (1x)` (control: `disabled (schedule)`);
- `show` works for both jobs;
- `enable` clears the reason and re-enables the job;
- no load errors.

Stable therefore tolerates the new value, and no tolerant reader has to ship first.

Accepted edges:
- A job whose fallbacks keep failing for their own reasons keeps retrying on its normal schedule. Those failures belong to their own classes, for example long provider rate-limit resets.
- An account retired in the middle of a run disables at the next run.
- Fallback chains that return an "exhausted" result instead of throwing are not classified (the production failures threw).
- The `auto-disabled` notice is delivered as a session event turn, like the existing auto-disable notices. If the owner session's own model cannot run (for example on the same signed-out account), that turn fails, and the notice does not reach the transcript. The job is still disabled with its recorded reason, which the automation list and `openclaw doctor` show.

## Evidence

- **Red on main, green here:** `src/cron/session-run.cross-provider-fallback.integration.test.ts` runs a recurring session-target automation whose recorded account was removed or replaced and which has no other model to run on. On the merge base, the job stays enabled after the failed run. On this branch, it is auto-disabled with `account-unavailable` and exactly one notice, and a second settled result sends nothing. The same file keeps the fallback-success cases `ok`, and keeps a job running when its fallback failed with a 429.
- **Isolated path:** `isolated-agent.auth-profile-propagation.test.ts` asserts the permanent classification for a removed account on both the embedded and CLI routes.
- **No over-trigger:** `timer-outcomes.regression.test.ts` keeps a job running when only the authorization owner changed.
- **Real Gateway** (built dist, isolated state, no real credentials): an automation recorded on an API-key account; the account was then logged out, and two runs were forced.
  - Merge base: the job stays enabled with 2 consecutive errors and a next run scheduled, and the person gets no notice.
  - This branch: after the first failure the job is disabled, with no next run and `autoDisabled.reason = account-unavailable`. One notice lands in the agent's conversation as a system notice.
- **Behavior suite** (real gpt-5.4-mini, 11 cases): 11/11 gating on this branch vs 10/11 on the merge base. The base miss is the subagent-spawn case, unrelated to cron.

fix(cron): wait for a provider's stated rate-limit reset before the next run (#207091)

## Problem

On a production deployment, 126 scheduled-automation runs in 7 days failed with "<model> is rate-limited. The provider says to retry in 5-6 days". Recurring jobs ran again on every slot, or hourly once the error backoff reached its 60-minute maximum, and every run hit the same limit. Two jobs were still looping with 25 consecutive errors. Nothing in the cron scheduler read the provider's reset time; a rate limit counted as a transient error.

## Fix

- The run result now carries the provider's reset time as a transient fact (`rateLimitResetAt`, never stored). It is set only when every failed model attempt was rate-limited with a known reset (candidates skipped for a local cooldown are ignored), and the earliest reset wins. It reuses the existing reset facts on the failover error.
  - Session-target jobs: the settled failure cause already reaches the automation settlement in-process.
  - Isolated jobs: the run's catch, forwarded by the isolated execution adapter.
- `applyJobResult` uses it when scheduling the next run after an error:
  - The next normal slot is the first scheduled slot at or after the reset, so cron expressions stay on their schedule.
  - A reset before the schedule's own next slot moves the quick retry to the reset. A later reset skips quick retries for the first slot after it (an off-slot time there would be moved earlier by schedule maintenance), and the failure alert is not held for a retry that is days away.
- One-shot jobs are unchanged.
- Jobs are not paused; the failure notice already names the reset time (#206945).

## User impact

A recurring automation on a model with a multi-day limit stops hitting the provider, or the local limit gate, every hour. It runs again on its first slot after the stated reset, and the user gets the failure alert once instead of after every slot.

## Evidence

- `src/cron/rate-limit-reset.integration.test.ts`: a loopback provider returns 429 with `retry-after: 518400`. On both the session-target and the isolated path, the run makes one provider request and reports the reset (~6 days). Fails on main (no reset reported), passes here.
- `src/cron/service/timer-outcomes.regression.test.ts`: an hourly `every` job and a weekday cron job land exactly on their first slot after the reset, schedule maintenance keeps that slot, and the failure alert is emitted. A 45-second reset moves the quick retry instead of skipping to the next day. Fails on main, passes here.
- The same file runs both execution adapters through the timer, schedule maintenance and the persisted store, including a 5-minute cron with a 20-minute reset: the stored next run is the first slot after the reset.
- Cron run, outcome, failure-alert and cross-provider fallback suites on both paths pass.

Accepted edge: a provider that states an absurd reset (for example years away) parks the job until then; the failure notice shows that date, and a reset the scheduler cannot represent is ignored.

fix(agents): apply the role model policy to every utility consumer (#207070)

## What problem this solves

Follow-up to #206962 (Activity recaps vs operator role model policy). The same role refusal reaches four other utility consumers, and the recap still retried its other owner refusals.

Real-user log signature (a production team Gateway; 331 on 2026-11-27):

```
[activity-summary] Activity recap deferred
  error: Your operator role cannot use this model. …
```

The Gateway's default role allows only main-chat models, so every utility model is refused for its sessions.

- **Progress narration** ignored the turn's role and ran the refused utility model (policy bypass).
- **The session observer** had no role check at all and ran the utility model for every session (bypass).
- **Titles** tried the refused utility model first, logged a false "Conversation label generation failed" warning, then made the regular-model pass.
- **The recap** turned "operator profile unavailable" and "role cannot access this agent" into a 120 s retry, re-run on every later activity.

## Change

`resolveUtilityModelSelectionForAgent` stays the one owner; each consumer now asks it with the relevant role:

- **Narrator:** uses the turn's `operatorAuthority`. A refusing role attaches no narrator. The narration completion carries the authority, so execution skips refused candidates in a partly allowed chain.
- **Observer:**
  - Resolves the session owner's role once per run through the recap's existing session-owner authority. The digest is persisted and shown to every viewer, so the owner's role applies.
  - An owner role that excludes the agent or refuses every utility model turns the run's observation off quietly: no degradation notice, no retry. A session whose owner profile was deleted still gets observation.
  - The authority reaches the completion.
- **Titles** (dashboard and channel thread): a refusing role makes no utility attempt and no warning. The documented regular-model title pass still runs; that is the session's own permitted model.
- **Recap:**
  - The authority returns a typed refusal instead of throwing.
  - A refusal ("profile gone", "role excludes the agent", "role refuses every utility model") publishes `unavailable` with no model call, no retry and no log line. The next activity asks again; a config or role change applies there with no extra state.
  - A role-changed read race keeps its existing retry.
- **Status and Doctor:**
  - When the Gateway substituted the agent's primary because no utility model is offered, `openclaw models status` shows `<model> (utility model not offered; using main model)`. A provider whose declared small model is the primary shows no note.
  - `openclaw doctor` reports the same line as an info finding.
  - No wire change.

## Not changed

- **Side chat:** it already makes no refused attempt. When the role refuses the utility route, it answers with the role's first permitted model, so a user's question is never refused.
- **Nothing offered at all** (`not-offered` with no listed primary): behavior unchanged from main.

## User population

- **Gateway:** multi-user Gateways whose operator roles refuse the utility models. Affected surfaces: narration in replies (`get-reply.ts` → `progress-narrator.ts`), observer digests (`session-observer.ts`), dashboard and thread titles, and Activity recaps.
- **Gateway and CLI:** `openclaw models status` and `openclaw doctor` users whose automatic utility routing falls back to the primary.

## Evidence

| Consumer | Main | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| Narrator, role allows only the main model | narrator attached; runs the refused utility model | options returned unchanged; no narration attempt |
| Observer, owner's role refuses the utility model | completion runs the utility model, no authority | refusal; 0 completions; the allowed case passes the owner's authority |
| Thread title, role allows only the main model | false "Conversation label generation failed" warning, then the main model | no warning; one completion on the main model |
| Recap, owner profile gone / role excludes the agent, 4 activity rounds 130 s apart | 120 s retry armed each round | 0 attempts, 0 retries; a committed config change lifts it on the next activity |
| Status, Gateway substituted the primary | `<model> (provider default)` | `<model> (utility model not offered; using main model)` |
| Status, provider's declared small model is the primary | - | `<model> (provider default)`; no note |
| Doctor, Gateway substituted the primary | - | info finding "utility model not offered; using main model" |

### Real CLI on an isolated Gateway

Each scenario runs its own Gateway (loopback port, empty `HOME` and state directory, `env -i`; no other OpenClaw state). The provider is a local fixture plugin, `w9-fixture`. Its manifest declares `defaultUtilityModel: "small"`, and its catalog `run` returns a `ready` outcome listing exactly the configured ids. `plugins.allow` holds only the fixture, so the published inventory is authoritative, as on a Gateway whose providers are all signed in. Base is this PR's merge base on `main` (`501ee911`); head is `ab1120a`. Same commands on both sides.

**(a) Utility model not offered.** Primary `w9-fixture/main`; the listing has only `main`. The Gateway publishes `{"modelRef":"w9-fixture/main","source":"provider-default"}` on both sides.

```text
# base: openclaw models status
Utility model : w9-fixture/main (provider default)
# base: openclaw doctor --lint --severity-min info --only core/doctor/model-references
(no findings)

# head: openclaw models status
Utility model : w9-fixture/main (utility model not offered; using main model)
# head: openclaw doctor --lint --severity-min info --only core/doctor/model-references
{"severity":"info","message":"utility model not offered; using main model","fixHint":"Configure agents.defaults.utilityModel with a model the catalog lists, or leave it unset to keep using the main model."}
```

**(b) The provider's declared small model is the primary.** Primary `w9-fixture/small`; the listing has `small` and `main`. Both sides print the same, with no note:

```text
# base and head: openclaw models status
Utility model : w9-fixture/small (provider default)
# base and head: openclaw doctor --lint --severity-min info --only core/doctor/model-references
(no findings)
```

An earlier head printed the note here from `doctor` only: Doctor has no current plugin metadata snapshot, so the declared model was invisible. `isUtilityModelNotOffered` now loads the manifests itself (`ab1120a`).

**(c) A role-policy refusal.** Primary `w9-fixture/main`; the listing has `main` and `small`. The default role `guest` allows only `w9-fixture/main`. The CLI connects as the token operator, so `models status` shows the agent's own selection (`w9-fixture/small (provider default)`) on both sides; a refused selection is not disclosed to a guest reader. The refusal and its reason come from config validation, identically on base and head:

```text
# base and head: openclaw doctor
[config] warnings: gateway.roles.definitions.guest.modelPolicy: Role "guest" allows no utility model for agent "main", so Activity recaps are off for sessions this role owns. Allow a utility model in this role's modelPolicy, or set a utilityModel the role allows.
```

Red on main (`501ee911`), green here: the recap "profile gone" and "role excludes the agent" cases (the retry was re-armed each round, with `Activity recap deferred` logged), and the title "no utility attempt or warning" case. The status and Doctor note is new; its tests cover the published wire shape and the declared-model false positive.

Checks on `ab1120adad`: touched suites green; `tsgo` core and test shards clean; oxlint, line-cap, session-identity and permission-read boundary checks clean; CI green. Local review: patch is correct, 0 findings.

Size: production about +200 lines; `list.status-command.ts` net −10 (the status field text moved to `list.status-utility.ts`).

fix(ai): every stream transport records a measured or explicitly unavailable context size (#207102)

## Problem

#207041 found that the Google stream completed turns without `usage.contextUsage`. The pre-request compaction check then re-estimated the whole history with its safety margin and compacted Gemini sessions early.

The same silent absence exists on main in other transports:
- **No measurement at all:** Mistral, Google Interactions and Radius.
- **No contextUsage when a turn completes without a usage report:** Anthropic, OpenAI Responses and Azure, the OpenAI ChatGPT route, Google Generative AI and Vertex, the Google plugin transport, Bedrock and Ollama.

Nothing checked this contract, so a new or changed transport could reintroduce early compaction silently.

## Fix

Contract: every bundled stream transport completes a turn with `usage.contextUsage` either `available`, from a field the provider measured, or explicitly `{ state: "unavailable" }`.

- `test/provider-context-usage-contract.test.ts` runs the real registered `streamSimple` for each built-in API against a fake upstream, plus each plugin-owned transport.
  - Each transport has a case with measured usage and a case without usage.
  - The test also asserts that the registered built-in APIs equal its rows, so a newly registered built-in fails until it has a row.
- Measured sources added, each named after the provider's response field:
  - Mistral: `usage.prompt_tokens` (cached tokens included).
  - Google Interactions: `usage.total_input_tokens` + `total_tool_use_tokens`.
  - Radius: a forwarded `usage.contextUsage` is kept as is; without one, Pi usage `input + cacheRead + cacheWrite`.
- Explicit `unavailable` when nothing was measured:
  - the shared `finalizeTransportStream`, which covers Anthropic, OpenAI Completions and Responses, Azure and Mistral;
  - the Google stream completion path and the Responses terminal (OpenAI Responses, Azure, ChatGPT);
  - Bedrock without a metadata event;
  - Ollama without provider counters, which previously left the field out.

Not a type-level requirement. The completed-message type is part of the public plugin SDK (`openclaw/plugin-sdk/llm`), and stored transcripts legitimately lack the field. Requiring it would break external plugin transports at compile time.

## Impact

- **Mistral and Google Interactions users:** compaction now starts from the measured request size instead of a padded re-estimate of the whole history, as for every other provider.
- **Turns with no usage report at all:** these are rare, since every provider normally reports usage. Such a turn is now an explicit zero-token `unavailable` marker, which the compaction check treats as a barrier, as it already does for OpenAI Completions and Anthropic. The next request re-estimates the history once, until the next measured turn re-anchors. That errs toward one early compaction, never an overflow. The status meter shows an estimate for that turn instead of a stale number.
- **Ollama turns with estimated counters:** these no longer count as provider measurements in compaction preparation or overflow checks.

## Evidence

- Contract test: main fails 15 of 30 cases; this branch passes 30 of 30. Each failure on main is `usage.contextUsage` received `undefined`.
- Touched transport suites green: 126, 149, 30 and 40 tests (Ollama, Bedrock, Radius, Google, Mistral, Interactions, shared transport).
- Updated consumer test: Ollama's counter cases expected the field to be absent when counters are missing; they now expect `unavailable`.
- Adversarial review: land with changes. Applied: Interactions measures only from the completed interaction's own usage, not a step's usage carried forward; a stray whitespace change was reverted.
- Local review: round 1 found that Radius replaced a forwarded context snapshot with its counters; fixed with a test. Round 2 on this head: patch is correct, 0 findings.
- The contract test reaches plugin transports through each plugin's `test-api` barrel, as the extension test boundary requires.
- Test-line allocation (`config/test-lines-allocations/207102-stream-context-usage-contract.txt`, 89 lines): the contract covers 15 transports in measured and unmeasured cases, each against its real fake upstream; that is the requested guard against a silent absence.

fix: converge plugins after every Gateway boot (#206926)

## What Problem This Solves

Plugin maintenance currently depends on an updater trial. Replacing OpenClaw through an image swap, global package install, manual Git pull, or standalone binary can leave installed plugins behind the serving core.

## User Impact

Every Gateway boot starts plugin convergence in the background after core readiness. Active trials defer the work. Changed plugins reload through the existing lifecycle; plugin failures do not delay readiness or change the core update outcome.

Boot maintenance is unattended and no longer inherits `openclaw update --accept-capabilities` consent from the trial. A plugin that widens capabilities is declined; the existing failed plugin step retains its capability-review guidance and exact `openclaw plugins update <id>` recovery command. Ordinary offline boots create no update run or failure notice.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Delete `maintainTrialPlugins` and the trial-keyed plugin scheduler; reuse the existing watcher, ten-minute child command, lifecycle lease, and batch reload.
- Use existing update history only to attribute completed plugin output to the serving build, never to decide whether convergence runs.
- Keep advisory Doctor inspections updater-only. The Docker entrypoint Doctor/capture deletion is deliberately outside this PR.
- No new persisted state, markers, statuses, notices, locks, flags, or retries.
- Runtime-only scope: **−4 production lines**, +63 unit-test lines, documentation updated. No survivor scenario, catalog, registry, or harness changes.

## Evidence

- Red on `ea77ca3d602c` in an isolated `ocx base --src`: ordinary/no-trial and offline boot cases fail because the plugin child is never called; pending/trial/restoring cases pass.
- The regression exercises the existing Gateway core-ready boundary, not a direct scheduler call.
- Merged-head stable-to-head gate: [Package Acceptance 46091303769](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46091303769), candidate `abbbf6eefa5701c63669eafaf89c23b28f0116f3`, baseline `openclaw@2026.11.10`, existing `update-restart-auth` lane.
- Baseline comparison: [current-main b7e36af75284 passed the same lane](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46086533588); [the old-base 42037bdcea59 candidate failed in old-updater Doctor admission](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46079640633). Current main `94ae31d8491d` is now merged before rerunning; the old-base failure is not classified as inherited or isolated to this change.
- The narrowed history guard preserves an already settled plugin step across later offline boots. All 3 focused owner regression cases passed; scoped core lint had 0 warnings and 0 errors.
- Earlier Docker seed CI reached its unchanged 55-minute outer limit after healthy, crash/rollback, and enforced downgrade receipts reported passing. No failing runtime assertion was recorded.
- The separate Doctor-free manual-swap proof PR #206999 is not a prerequisite for this runtime PR or PR 4.
- Review findings are repaired or explicitly rejected: ordinary failures use the existing warning log, notice errors cannot skip convergence, live details refresh, and settled history is not rewritten. Trial consent remains intentionally absent from this boot job.
- Current-head hosted validation is pending. No local full build was run; the stalled Boat wrapper was cancelled before allocation.

fix(codex): list the model catalog again when the reported account changes (#207089)

## Problem

`test/plugins/codex-model-catalog.gateway.test.ts` fails on main since #206994 (`expected 2 to be greater than 2`). It passes at #206994's parent.

#206994 reuses a Codex `model/list` discovery for the same client, the same account revision and 300 s. The revision advances on `account/updated` and on login, logout and config writes. An app-server that OpenClaw does not own (user-home mode over a socket, or a proxy) can switch accounts without sending `account/updated`. The catalog then kept serving the previous account's model list and account type for up to 5 minutes, even for `models.list refresh: true`.

## Fix

The memo owner (`extensions/codex/src/app-server/model-catalog.ts`) now reads `account/read` first (`refreshToken: false`, no `/models` fetch). It reuses a discovery only if Codex reports the same account as when it listed. The other reuse conditions stay: same client, account revision and scope, within 300 s.

The account response includes ChatGPT `userId` and workspace routing, so two workspaces of one email are told apart. The slow call that #206994 avoids, `model/list`, which refetches `/models`, is still skipped on a warm turn.

## Security check

A list cached for one credential cannot be served for another:
- The shared client key includes the auth profile, the auth binding fingerprint, the prepared auth, the auth requirement and native auth. A different credential or auth mode therefore uses a different client, and reuse requires the same client.
- `account/updated` advances the revision (`client.ts:656`).
- The gap fixed here is a silent account switch inside an app-server OpenClaw does not own.

## Impact

- Codex-runtime users on an app-server that switches accounts outside OpenClaw: the catalog follows the reported account on the next load, not up to 5 minutes later.
- Warm turns: one local `account/read` RPC instead of none. `model/list` and its `/models` refetch stay skipped, so the #206994 gain holds.

## Evidence

- Gateway test: passes at `f31a6781^`, fails on main `49c5e3ea`, passes on this branch (1/1, 300 s timeout, run alone).
- New unit test: one client and revision, accounts a, a, b, b, a. It lists exactly `[a, b, a]`. Red on main (main lists once), green here (model-catalog unit files 20/20 and 2/2).
- Known limit: two API-key accounts report the same `account/read`, so a silent key-to-key switch on an unowned server still waits for the 300 s TTL.
- Real Codex can switch accounts without `account/updated`: `AuthManager::auth()` reloads external auth on every call, and the remote-control and apps reloads update cached auth silently.
- Adversarial review: safe to land. Local review on this head: patch is correct, 0 findings.

feat(status): say when the last request sent no prompt cache key (#207050)

## Problem
An OpenAI-style route that is not declared to accept `prompt_cache_key` gets no cache key. Nothing tells the user. A relay user cannot see why cache hits are low or that one config line would opt in.

## Change
- The prompt-cache tracker records, for each session's latest request, whether the wire body carried `prompt_cache_key`. It records this even when the provider reports no cache usage, which is common on relays. `readLastPromptCacheKeyFact(sessionKey)` exposes the fact, addressed by the chat key (session-identity ratchet) (`prompt-cache-observability.ts`).
- `/status` adds `· cache key: not sent` to the Endpoint row only when that recorded request went to the selected model on an OpenAI-style API (Chat Completions or Responses) without a key. `/status` applies no second rule: providers that opt in at run time (Together, Fireworks, xAI, …) show nothing, because their requests carry the key.
- Privacy: the note is a fixed phrase. The endpoint URL still goes through `formatModelEndpointUrl`: credentials and custom paths are stripped, and a suppressed endpoint stays `unknown`. The note may sit beside `unknown` (`unknown · cache key: not sent`), because a real Gateway shows custom relays as `Endpoint: unknown` today; tying the note to a visible URL would hide it from exactly the users it is for.
- Docs: opt in with `compat.supportsPromptCacheKey: true` only if the endpoint accepts `prompt_cache_key`; remove it if requests fail with HTTP 400. Many providers cache automatically.

## User impact
- Undeclared relay: `🌐 Endpoint: unknown · cache key: not sent` (or the sanitized URL when `/status` shows one).
- Every other route: unchanged.
- No request bytes change.

## Evidence
- Owner test (`prompt-cache-observability.test.ts`): real `prepareProviderPrompt` bodies; recorded without usage; keyless → `false`, keyed → `true`.
- Status test (`status-text.test.ts`): a keyless request to the selected relay model shows the note; a keyed request or a different model does not.
- Message test: a relay URL with a custom path and token shows as `https://relay.example/[path hidden] · cache key: not sent`; a suppressed endpoint shows `unknown · cache key: not sent` and nothing from the URL. (Credential stripping is covered by the existing endpoint test.)
- Real Gateway e2e (throwaway, not committed): one Gateway, fake OpenAI-compatible relay on loopback, two agents. Each sends a real turn, then `/status`. The relay saw `gpt-5.4-mini` with no `prompt_cache_key` and `declared-model` (compat `supportsPromptCacheKey: true`) with a key. `/status` showed `Endpoint: unknown · cache key: not sent` for the first and `Endpoint: unknown` for the second.

## Known limits (Fable review, documented)
- The note reflects the last *completed* request. It is not shown while a turn runs, and it updates only after the next request; the docs say so.
- Facts are in memory: after a Gateway restart there is no note until the next request. Harnesses that do not record (Codex app-server) show no note.
- `cacheRetention: "none"` and an explicit `supportsPromptCacheKey: false` also produce "not sent"; the docs list all three causes.

fix: let the end-of-turn recovery request reuse the turn's cached prompt (#207052)

## What Problem This Solves

When a turn ends with only `NO_REPLY` after tool calls and the run needs a result, OpenClaw sends one recovery request that asks the model for the final answer. Today that request has an empty system prompt and no tools, and it uses its own cache key. It is the only request of the session with that shape, so it reads none of the turn's cached prefix, and its reply (with thinking on Claude models) is produced under a different prefix from every other request in the session. On a long-running assistant install with Claude models, 3 of 15 sessions contained such recovery replies (25 in total).

## User Impact

On OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages, through the Gateway and `openclaw agent --local` alike (both run `prepareTerminalWithSettledTurnFinalization`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run-loop.ts:531`), the recovery request is now the turn's last request (system prompt, tools, model, thinking settings, cache key and history, byte for byte) plus the recovery instruction, with `tool_choice: none`. It reads the turn's cached prefix instead of starting cold, and the model still cannot call a tool, as today.

- Both protocols are the ones already declared cache-neutral for `tool_choice` (`isToolChoiceCacheNeutral`, measured in #206937), so changing only `tool_choice` keeps the cached prefix.
- On Anthropic, if the thinking binding includes `tool_choice`, the reply's thinking drops on later requests, the same as on main. That has not been measured; it is never worse than main.
- Other protocols, and every case where the turn's request cannot be reused (context refused by the provider, a different model, a continuation-only request, or a history that does not end with the turn's last item), keep today's tool-free request.

No config, schema or stored-data change.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The repository rule: a side request that reuses the conversation shares the turn's request preparation.
- The recovery runs as one more attempt of the same run, so the run's provider prompt state still holds the turn's last prepared provider body. Session forks already replay that body. The recovery now replays it too (`readSettledTurnRequest`, `applySettledTurnRequest`), with `tool_choice: none` in the protocol's existing wire shape (the fork's `TOOL_CHOICE_NONE` table). The fork's "write prepared request plus suffix" code is shared (`sendPreparedItems`). No provider, model or API branch is added.
- The recovery renders earlier history without the turn's envelopes (timestamp prefix, runtime-context wrapper), so the fork's every-item match never matches it. The recovery instead appends its own items after the item equal to the turn's last sent item. After a tool loop that item is a tool result with a unique call id.
- Known edge: if the turn's last item were an id-less message that also appeared earlier, the anchor could land early. Recovery only runs after settled tool turns, whose last item is a tool result.

## Evidence

- New test `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner.settled-recovery-prefix.test.ts`: the real runner with a fake provider fetch, synthetic placeholder content only (thinking block `<placeholder>`, signature `sig-1`).
  - On main: red. The recovery request's system prompt hashes to an empty prompt (Anthropic and Responses).
  - On this branch: the recovery request's system prompt, tools, model, thinking and cache key, and every parameter except `tool_choice`, hash the same as the turn's last request. Its history is byte-identical to the turn's (for Responses, the effective input of the `previous_response_id` chain) up to the new user message. Both protocols send `tool_choice: none`.
- Existing suites green: `session-fork-request.test.ts`, `attempt-stream-settle.test.ts`, `settled-turn-finalization.test.ts`, `settled-turn-finalization.transport.test.ts`, `embedded-agent-runner.run-embedded-agent.finalization-scope.test.ts`, `agent-tools.prefix-stability.test.ts`, `harness/builtin-openclaw.test.ts`.
- Not proven here: whether the reply's thinking stays bound when later turns replay it. That needs a real Anthropic request, and this change uses no paid key. The existing 25 replies are unchanged.

fix(agents): freeze every embedded dispatch and let harnesses declare who builds the prompt (#207022)

## Problem

#206969 stopped a fallback model from failing a turn that an earlier model had already sent without a frozen model prompt (a "projection"). It did that by tolerating the missing projection for every harness. That tolerance also hid real gaps in the embedded runner, which is supposed to freeze every turn before sending it:

- An inter-session message (`sessions_send`) whose text was unchanged was sent without a projection. This is the case that failed a production turn.
- A turn that compaction removed from the request (a keyless turn) was sent without a projection.

## Fix

- Harnesses declare who builds the prompt with a new optional field, `promptProjection: "captures" | "external"`. The default is `"external"`, so undeclared third-party harnesses behave as before.
  - The built-in embedded harness declares `"captures"`. Codex declares `"external"`, because its app-server builds its own turn input.
  - The harness lifecycle records the declaration for one attempt only. The first send locks it in, and an attempt that never sent clears it.
- After a `"captures"` send, a late capture is an error again. The #206969 tolerance now applies only to `"external"` sends.
- The embedded runner makes that true. Unchanged inter-session text is now frozen too. Before the first send of an attempt, a turn that the prompt transform could not project is frozen as its own transcript text, so no fallback ever re-captures it.
- The new field is documented in `docs/plugins/sdk-agent-harness/core-ownership.md`.

## User impact

None visible on the normal path. A turn the embedded runner sends now always carries the text the provider received, so a later fallback on any harness replays the same bytes. Third-party harnesses that do not declare the field keep the current behavior.

## Evidence

- Red on main, green here:
  - The compacted keyless turn is frozen before dispatch, and the retained turn keeps no projection.
  - Inter-session turns are stored with their sent envelope (plain, forwarded and hook bodies).
- A built-in (`"captures"`) send without a projection makes a later capture throw; an undeclared harness keeps the tolerance.
- An attempt that never sent cannot apply its `"captures"` declaration to a later send outside the lifecycle.
- Projection and fallback suites on both routes pass: embedded submit, context and boundary, the recorder, the harness lifecycle, and the Codex app-server prompt projection.

fix(google): record the measured context size so Gemini sessions compact at their real occupancy (#207041)

## Problem

`test/prompt-cache-prefix-stability.google.e2e.test.ts` is red on main (`expected 2 to be 1`). An unrelated chat on a 64,000-token window receives 24 tool results of 8,000 characters each. It compacts twice inside that run (requests 14 and 25), where Anthropic, Bedrock and both OpenAI transports compact once. Every PR that runs this lane needs an override.

The same cause reaches Gemini users: their sessions compact before their context is full.

## Root cause

`packages/ai/src/providers/google-stream.ts` fills `usage` from `usageMetadata` but never sets `usage.contextUsage`. Every other transport records the measured request size there:
- Anthropic: `anthropic-usage.ts`
- OpenAI Responses and Completions: `openai-transport-shared.ts`
- Bedrock: `extensions/amazon-bedrock/stream.runtime.ts`

The pre-request pressure check (`preemptive-compaction.ts`, `resolveProviderContextBoundary`) starts from the last assistant turn's measured `contextUsage` and estimates only what came after it. A Gemini turn has none. So every check re-estimated the entire history locally, with the 1.2 safety margin, and crossed the compaction threshold well before the real occupancy.

## Fix

At the Google stream owner, record `contextUsage` once the terminal chunk reports a prompt count:
- `promptTokens` = `promptTokenCount` (Gemini includes cached content in it) + `toolUsePromptTokenCount`
- `totalTokens` = prompt tokens + candidate tokens + thought tokens

Before the terminal chunk, or with no prompt count, it is `unavailable`, as on the other transports.

The journey had one known break for Google, "the pressure check trims tool results that earlier requests already sent". That trim did not occur on main either: main's only breaks in that chat are compactions. Per the journey's own rule ("a known break that no longer occurs has landed: remove its entry"), the entry is removed, with its now-unused matcher helpers and unit case. The journey is stricter: any trim now fails it.

## Impact

- Gemini (Google Generative AI) users on the embedded runtime, through the Gateway and in one-shot runs: the compaction decision uses the size Google measured, as on every other provider, instead of a padded local re-estimate. Long sessions with large tool results compact later and less often, and keep more detail.
- Status and session usage readers now get Gemini's measured context size, the same as for other providers.

## Evidence

- `packages/ai/src/providers/google-shared.test.ts`: red on main `8b36e346` (2 failed / 35: no `contextUsage`), green on this branch (35/35). Cases cover a measured terminal report with cache and tool-use tokens, sparse usage with no prompt count, and a non-terminal report.
- `test/prompt-cache-prefix-known-breaks.test.ts`: 2/2; test-root typecheck clean.
- Main's CI log (Bun shard) for the journey lists three breaks in the unrelated chat. Two are compactions inside the overflow run: 125 KB at request 14, then 114 KB at request 25. The third is the explicit compaction. None of them is a trim.
- CI on this head: all five prefix-stability journeys pass, Google included (86 s). Local review: patch is correct, 0 findings.
